Let $\gamma$ be standard Gaussian measure, let $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ be the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis, and let $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ have coefficients $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $b_m=\int g h_m\,d\gamma$. For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, let $(X,Y)$ have the centered bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_mb_m\rho^m.$$
The series is absolutely convergent, including at $\rho=\pm1$. In particular, the Gaussian dual kernel of $f$ is $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2\rho^m$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$.

thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-pro.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

cor-iid-finite-variance-weak-law.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

cor-mean-value-theorem.interface:
## Statement

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

def-convergence-in-probability.interface:
## Definition

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

def-neural-tangent-kernel.interface:
## Definition

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

def-width-normalized-fully-connected-net.interface:
## Definition

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

thm-countably-exceptional-differentiabil.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable except at countably
many points, and $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, then $F$ is absolutely continuous and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt$$
for every $x\in[a,b]$.

thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gra.interface:
## Statement

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

lem-bivariate-gaussian-feature-expectati.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $C_n$ be real symmetric positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ matrices converging entrywise to $C$, and suppose both diagonal entries of $C_n$ and of $C$ are positive. Let $(U_n,V_n)$ and $(U,V)$ have centered bivariate normal laws with covariance matrices $C_n$ and $C$, respectively; singular covariance matrices are allowed. For every globally Lipschitz $\tau:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[\tau(U_n)\tau(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[\tau(U)\tau(V)].$$
For every bounded Borel function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[g(U_n)g(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[g(U)g(V)].$$
The second conclusion applies to any bounded measurable representative of an almost-everywhere derivative, including when the limiting pair is supported on a line.

lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multiva.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

lem-fixed-time-lazy-training-stability.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Fix a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a horizon $T\ge0$. Let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz, twice continuously differentiable, and have bounded second derivative. Use the network parameterization and independent standard-normal initialization in the width-normalized network definition, with scalar output $n_L=1$. For each hidden-width tuple $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, suppose a differentiable parameter path exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)\,d_i(t),$$

where $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable. Write $K_t=(K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$ for the finite-data scalar neural tangent kernel. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_N\,dt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential hidden-width limit, where $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$ and stochastic boundedness means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ satisfies the iterated-limit upper bound $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)<\varepsilon$. Then, as $n_1\to\infty$ first and then $n_2,\ldots,n_{L-1}\to\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

thm-absolutely-continuous-functions-have.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

lem-biased-hermite-kernel-is-strictly-po.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Fix an integer $n_0\ge1$, a number $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. Let $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, put $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2$, and define $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q\,z)$. Let $a_m=\int \mu(z)h_m(z)\,d\gamma(z)$ be its coefficients in the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ of standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$. For $x,y\in S^{n_0-1}$, let $(U_{x,y},V_{x,y})$ be a centered Gaussian pair with variances $q$ and covariance $\beta^2+x\cdot y/n_0$, and set $k(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{x,y})\sigma(V_{x,y})]+\beta^2$. Then $k$ is strictly positive definite on $S^{n_0-1}$: for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)>0$. The conclusion includes $n_0=1$, for which the sphere consists of the two points $-1$ and $1$.

lem-gaussian-activation-covariance-stric.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have the centered multivariate normal law with covariance $C$, let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz and nonconstant, and let $\beta>0$. Let $s$ be a bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$: it agrees with the ordinary derivative wherever that derivative exists, and its values on the remaining Lebesgue-null set are arbitrary. Define
$$S_{ij}:=\mathbb E[\sigma(Z_i)\sigma(Z_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad D_{ij}:=\mathbb E[s(Z_i)s(Z_j)]\quad(1\le i,j\le m).$$
Then $S$ is strictly positive definite and $D$ is positive semidefinite. Consequently, for every positive-semidefinite matrix $T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, the matrix $T\circ D+S$ is strictly positive definite, where $\circ$ denotes entrywise multiplication.

thm-sequential-infinite-width-ntk-limit.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Fix a finite list $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Let $s$ be any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$, meaning that it agrees with the ordinary derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set; such a representative exists and is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. For every tuple of positive integer hidden widths $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, use the width-normalized network with independent standard-normal initialization and scalar linear output.

Put

$$\Sigma^1_{ij}=\frac{x_i\cdot x_j}{n_0}+\beta^2.$$

For $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U_i,U_j)$ have the centered Gaussian law with variances $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii},\Sigma^{r-1}_{jj}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ij}$, and define

$$\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad \dot\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[s(U_i)s(U_j)].$$

These Gaussian laws may be singular; their marginal variances are at least $\beta^2$, and their laws and expectations depend only on the displayed covariance. Define $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and, for $r=2,\ldots,L$,

$$\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij},\qquad K_\infty=(\Theta^L_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N.$$

At initialization, the finite-data neural tangent Gram matrix $K_0$ converges in probability to $K_\infty$ under the sequential hidden-width limit $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}$.

For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative, that $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable, and that for each width tuple a differentiable parameter path $\theta(t)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ makes the iterated-limit upper bound on $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)$ less than $\varepsilon$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Along the path,

$$\dot f_t(x_i)=-\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K_t(i,j)d_j(t),$$

and

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|f_t-f_0+\frac1N\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\right\|_N\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$

Thus the finite-time output equation has the deterministic limiting kernel as its generator in the precise integrated-error sense displayed above.

prop-ntk-positive-definite-on-the-sphere.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. For $x,y$ on the unit sphere $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, define $\Sigma^1(x,y)=x\cdot y/n_0+\beta^2$. Recursively, for $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U,V)$ be a centered Gaussian pair whose covariance entries are $\Sigma^{r-1}(x,x),\Sigma^{r-1}(y,y),\Sigma^{r-1}(x,y)$, and set

$$\Sigma^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U)\sigma(V)]+\beta^2,\qquad D^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[s(U)s(V)],$$

where $s$ is any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$. Set $\Theta^1=\Sigma^1$ and $\Theta^r(x,y)=\Theta^{r-1}(x,y)D^r(x,y)+\Sigma^r(x,y)$. Then for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^{n_0-1}$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$,

$$\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_ic_j\Theta^L(x_i,x_j)>0.$$

Thus the scalar limiting neural tangent kernel is strictly positive definite on every finite set of distinct sphere points, for every $n_0\ge1$ and $L\ge2$. In dimension $n_0=1$ this includes both antipodal points of $S^0=\{-1,1\}$.

thm-least-squares-ntk-mode-decay.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC and use the source-normalized network with scalar output, a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N$, and limiting neural tangent Gram matrix $K_\infty$ from the sequential infinite-width theorem. For a target vector $y\in\mathbb R^N$, consider the finite-data least-squares loss $\mathcal L(f)=\frac1{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N(f_i-y_i)^2$ and its limiting kernel-gradient-flow equation

$$\dot f(t)=-\frac1N K_\infty(f(t)-y),\qquad f(0)=f_0.$$

Let $K_\infty=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)Q^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\lambda_i\ge0$. Then for every $t\ge0$,

$$\bigl(Q^T(f(t)-y)\bigr)_i=e^{-t\lambda_i/N}\,\bigl(Q^T(f_0-y)\bigr)_i\quad(1\le i\le N).$$

Zero-eigenvalue residual components remain constant. If the inputs are pairwise distinct points on $S^{n_0-1}$, with $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation, then $K_\infty$ is positive definite and $f(t)\to y$ as $t\to\infty$.

def-frobenius-matrix-norm.interface:
## Definition

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

## Remarks

- **The name records the entry-sum definition.** Different sources write
  $\lVert A\rVert_F$, $\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}$, or
  $\lVert A\rVert_{2,\mathrm{HS}}$; this library uses $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$
  exclusively and does not fold it into the induced $p$-norm notation.

- **Zero-sized shapes are included.** At $m=0$ or $n=0$ the double sum is the
  empty sum $0$, so the unique empty matrix has Frobenius norm $0$; this is the
  value of the inner-product norm of the zero space.

def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensiona.interface:
## Definition

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

thm-operator-norm-is-the-largest-singula.interface:
## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

def-rademacher-complexity.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

def-sample-covering-number.interface:
## Definition

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-.interface:
## Statement

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

def-hyperbolic-functions.interface:
## Definition

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivative.interface:
## Statement

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

thm-jensen-inequality-for-expectation.interface:
## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

def-natural-logarithm.interface:
## Definition

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

## Remarks

The domain is exactly $(0,\infty)$. This definition assigns no real logarithm to $0$ or to a negative number.

thm-natural-logarithm-laws.interface:
## Statement

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

def-borel-sigma-algebra.interface:
## Definition

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-produc.interface:
## Statement

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

def-multiclass-margin-ramp-loss.interface:
## Definition

Let $K\ge2$, let $D$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^K$ be a continuous score map. At $(x,y)$ its **multiclass margin** is
$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is the smallest index maximizing $F(x)_j$. Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le j\le K}F(x)_j\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The score coordinates are continuous, and finite maxima, comparisons, and the piecewise-linear ramp preserve Borel measurability. Thus the classification event and ramp loss in the displayed integrals are Borel sets or functions, so the risks are well-defined for $D$.

def-identically-distributed-and-iid-rand.interface:
## Definition

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

thm-mcdiarmid-bounded-differences.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

thm-independent-random-elements-have-pro.interface:
## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation.interface:
## Statement

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

lem-probability-measure-basic-identities.interface:
## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

lem-spectral-network-matrix-cover.interface:
## Statement

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ with $n,d,m\ge1$, and let $a,s\ge0$. Suppose
$$C:=\{A\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}:\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a,\ \lVert A\rVert_\sigma\le s\}$$
is nonempty. Put $U:=\{XA:A\in C\}$. For every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2dm).$$
If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$ or $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, then $N_F(U,\epsilon)=1$. Here $\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}$ is the column-sum norm of the transpose-difference, as fixed in the spectral-network-complexity definition, and $N_F$ is the proper Frobenius covering number.

thm-singular-value-decomposition.interface:
## Statement

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

lem-spectral-network-output-covering-ent.interface:
## Statement

Fix an architecture and activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition, with widths $d_0,ldots,d_L$ and $W:=\max_i d_i$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_0}$ be any sample matrix, let $M_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$, and fix $s_i>0$ and $b_i\ge0$. Suppose each feasible layer set
$$C_i:=\{A_i:\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i,\ \lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i\}$$
is nonempty. Let $\mathcal H_X$ be the set of $n\times d_L$ score matrices whose $r$th row is $F_A(x_r)^\top$, for $A_i\in C_i$ and the $r$th row $x_r^\top$ of $X$. Then for every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(\mathcal H_X,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2W^2)\left(\prod_{i=1}^L(\rho_i s_i)^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^3.$$
The logarithm is natural, an empty product equals $1$, and $N_F$ uses proper centers in the covered score-matrix set.

lem-empirical-rademacher-covering-integr.interface:
## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a fixed sample, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions into $[0,1]$. Write $\mathcal G|S$ for the set of column vectors $(g(z_1),\ldots,g(z_n))^\top$ as $g$ ranges over $\mathcal G$. For $0<\alpha\le\sqrt n$,
$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\frac{4\alpha}{\sqrt n}+\frac{12}{n}\int_\alpha^{\sqrt n}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon)}\,d\epsilon,$$
where $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S$ is the one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity with $1/n$ normalization and $N_F$ is the proper Frobenius covering number of the sample-vector set, identified with $n\times1$ matrices. The set $\mathcal G|S$ is totally bounded because it lies in $[0,1]^n$.

lem-multiclass-margin-rademacher-general.interface:
## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice.

Fix a finite network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, output size $K=d_L\ge2$, and activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Let $s_i>0$, $b_i\ge0$, and reference matrices $M_i$ be such that the class
$$\mathcal F:=\{F_A:\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i,\ \lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i\text{ for every }i\}$$
is nonempty. Let $D$ be any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an independent identically distributed sample from $D$ with $n\ge1$, and fix $\gamma>0$ and $0<\delta<1$. Define the ramp-loss class
$$\mathcal L_\gamma:=\{(x,y)\mapsto\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y)):F\in\mathcal F\}.$$
With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$, every $F\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
$$L_0(F)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F)+2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}},$$
where $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S$ is the one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity with $1/n$ normalization.

lem-bounded-spectral-class-margin-genera.interface:
## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice.

Fix a finite network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, output size $K=d_L\ge2$, activations, and reference matrices as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Let $s_i>0$, $b_i\ge0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be the nonempty class with layer constraints $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ and $\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i$. Let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an iid sample from any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, let $X$ be its input matrix with rows $x_i^\top$, and fix $n\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and $0<\delta<1$. Set $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, every $F_A\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
$$L_0(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)+\frac8n+\frac{36\sqrt{20}\,\lVert X\rVert_F\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\log n}{\gamma n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.$$
All logarithms are natural. The matrix norm on $X$ is the Frobenius norm, and the empirical margin loss uses the threshold convention $m_{F_A}(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma$.

thm-product-of-countable.interface:
## Statement

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

thm-spectral-margin-bound-for-multiclass.interface:
## Statement

Assume the axiom of choice. Fix a network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, $K=d_L\ge2$, zero-bias recurrence and zero-origin $\rho_i$-Lipschitz activations as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Fix reference matrices $M_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i\times d_{i-1}}$. Let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an iid sample of size $n\ge1$ from any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $X$ be the matrix with rows $x_r^\top$. Fix $0<\delta<1$ and set $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every network with nonzero layer matrices and every margin $\gamma>0$,
$$L_0(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)+\frac8n+\frac{72\sqrt{20}\,(1+\lVert X\rVert_F)\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\log n}{\gamma n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L\left[\left(\frac1L+\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\right)\prod_{r\ne i}\left(\frac1L+\lVert A_r\rVert_\sigma\right)\right]^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}+3\sqrt{\frac{Q(A,X,\gamma,n,\delta)}{2n}},$$
where all logarithms are natural, an empty product equals $1$, and
$$\begin{aligned}Q(A,X,\gamma,n,\delta):={}&\log(6/\delta)+\log(2+n\gamma)+\log(2+n/\gamma)+2\log(2+\lVert X\rVert_F)\\&+2\sum_{i=1}^L\log\!\left(2+L\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\right)+2\sum_{i=1}^L\log\!\left(2+L\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\right).
\end{aligned}$$

def-measurable-space.interface:
## Definition

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-pr.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from [[def-measurable-pointwise-extended-real-product]], and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]]. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

def-margin-preserving-compression.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable instance space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have its discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, and equip $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ and its finite powers with their product sigma-algebras. Let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$. For an integer $m\ge1$, write a sample as $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$. A score map $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_K):\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ is **coordinatewise measurable** when each $u_k:(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Define its classifier by the least-index tie rule

$$h_u(x):=\min\{k\in\mathcal Y:u_k(x)=\max_{j\in\mathcal Y}u_j(x)\}$$

and its margin on label $y$ by

$$M_u(x,y):=u_y(x)-\max_{j\in\mathcal Y,\ j\ne y}u_j(x).$$

For each $k\in\mathcal Y$,
$$\{x:h_u(x)=k\}=\bigcap_{j<k}\{x:u_k(x)>u_j(x)\}\cap\bigcap_{j>k}\{x:u_k(x)\ge u_j(x)\},$$
and each comparison set is measurable; an intersection over no indices means $\mathcal X$. Since $\mathcal Y$ is finite, $M_u$ is measurable on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ as well. The population zero-one risk is
$$R_P(h_u):=P\{(x,y):h_u(x)\ne y\}.$$
For a sample $S$ of length $m$ and $\gamma\ge0$, the empirical margin loss is
$$\widehat L_\gamma(u;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_u(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The event defining $R_P(h_u)$ is measurable by measurability of $h_u$.

Fix integers $q\ge0$ and $r\ge1$. A fixed-helper finite parameter codebook consists of a helper string $s$ fixed independently of the sample, finite nonempty sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$, and one coordinatewise measurable decoder score map $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ for each $a\in\mathcal A$. For $q=0$, the empty product is the singleton containing the empty tuple. The codebook and all its decoders are fixed independently of the sample, so $|\mathcal A|\le r^q$.

Let $F:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for the product sigma-algebra on its domain and the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^K$. Let $\alpha:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable, where $\mathcal A$ has its discrete sigma-algebra, and write $f_S(x):=F(S,x)$. For $\epsilon>0$, the sample-dependent trained score map $f_S$ is $\epsilon$-compressible by this codebook on a sample $S$ if
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m).$$
The code $\alpha(S)$ may depend on $S$; the helper string, codebook, and decoders remain fixed independently of the sample.

lem-bounded-variable-hoeffding-mgf.interface:
## Statement

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

lem-measurable-functions-preserve-indepe.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variabl.interface:
## Statement

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing.interface:
## Statement

The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions.interface:
## Statement

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

thm-composition-of-continuous-functions.interface:
## Statement

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-elem.interface:
## Definition

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

cor-expectation-of-an-indicator-is-proba.interface:
## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

thm-finite-description-compression-bound.interface:
## Statement

The following corrected finite-description form of Arora, Ge, Neyshabur, and Zhang's compression bound applies to a measurable sample-dependent score classifier. Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have the discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, put $\Sigma_Z=\Sigma_X\otimes2^{\mathcal Y}$ on $Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, and let $P$ be a probability law on $(Z,\Sigma_Z)$. Let $m\ge1$ and draw $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$ independently and identically distributed (IID) with law $P$, with sample space $Z^m$ carrying $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}$. Fix integers $q\ge0$, $r\ge1$, a helper string $s$ independent of $S$, finite nonempty parameter sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$ (with the empty product a singleton when $q=0$), a distortion tolerance $\epsilon>0$, and a confidence level $0<\delta<1$. For any score map $u$ with measurable coordinates, write $h_u(x)$ for the classifier that chooses the least index attaining the largest coordinate of $u(x)$. For each $a\in\mathcal A$, let $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ have measurable coordinates and put $h_{s,a}:=h_{g_{s,a}}$. Equip $\mathbb R^K$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Let $F:Z^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}\otimes\Sigma_X$, write $f_S(x)=F(S,x)$, and let $\alpha:Z^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable for the discrete sigma-algebra on $\mathcal A$. Suppose that, for $P^m$-almost every $S$,
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m)$$
With natural logarithms, define
$$R_P(h):=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\},\qquad \widehat R_S(h):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\},$$
$$M_{f_S}(x,y):=f_S(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}f_S(x)_j,\qquad \widehat L_\gamma(f_S;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\},\qquad \gamma\ge0.$$
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,
$$R_P\bigl(h_{s,\alpha(S)}\bigr)\le\widehat L_{2\epsilon}(f_S;S)+\sqrt{\frac{q\log r+\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}.$$
In particular, the coordinatewise distortion $\epsilon$ only guarantees preservation of an observed label when its original score margin is strictly greater than $2\epsilon$. The conclusion bounds the selected compressed classifier $h_{s,\alpha(S)}$; it does not bound the original classifier $h_{f_S}$ unless a separate all-domain loss-preservation argument is supplied. The theorem assumes a suitable fixed-helper compressor and makes no claim that a network compression construction exists or that layer-stability or cushion hypotheses hold.

cor-second-derivative-characterises-conv.interface:
## Statement

If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules.interface:
## Statement

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

lem-mean-value-theorem-on-closed-interva.interface:
## Statement

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral.interface:
## Statement

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

lem-cauchy-schwarz-for-finite-random-var.interface:
## Statement

For real random variables $X,Y$ on a finite probability space,
$$\mathbb E[XY]^2\le\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Y^2].$$
No equality characterization is asserted on outcomes of probability zero.

def-moments-variance-and-covariance.interface:
## Definition

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

lem-contrastive-hinge-and-logistic-loss-.interface:
## Statement

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm and $\log_2 u:=\ln(u)/\ln(2)$ for $u>0$. Define the one-negative hinge and logistic losses by $\ell_{\rm h}(t):=(1+t)_+$ and $\ell_{\rm log}(t):=\log_2(1+e^t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, where $r_+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Put $L_0:=1+1/\ln(2)$. Each loss is convex, nondecreasing, $L_0$-Lipschitz, and has value $1$ at $0$. For $R>0$ and either loss $\ell$, define $B_{\ell,R}:=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$. Then $0<B_{\ell,R}\le4L_0R^2$.

def-latent-class-contrastive-learning.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal C_0,\rho)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable probability spaces. For each class $c\in\mathcal C$, let $D_c$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and assume $c\mapsto D_c(A)$ is measurable for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-fi.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector.interface:
## Definition

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

lem-vector-rademacher-contraction-for-bo.interface:
## Statement

Let $m,d\ge1$, let $V$ be a nonempty bounded subset of $(\mathbb R^d)^m$, and let $h_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz for one common $L\ge0$. Let $(\varepsilon_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $(\eta_{it})_{1\le i\le m,1\le t\le d}$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Writing $v_i=(v_{i1},\ldots,v_{id})$, the one-sided averages satisfy

$$\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{v\in V}\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i h_i(v_i)\le\sqrt3L\,\mathbb E_\eta\sup_{v\in V}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{t=1}^d\eta_{it}v_{it}.$$

Neither supremum uses an absolute value, and no condition $h_i(0)=0$ is imposed. The bound holds for finite or infinite bounded $V$; all displayed suprema are finite.

thm-rademacher-uniform-generalization.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. Take $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ to be the coordinate sample with law $P^m$. Put $P_mg=m^{-1}\sum_i g(Z_i)$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}:=\{1-g:g\in\mathcal G\}$. Assume the sample, independent-copy and sign suprema over $\mathcal G$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}$ used in the displayed claims and the symmetrization argument are measurable. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs, and let

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(Z_i),\qquad \mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G),$$

where the $\sigma_i$ are independent uniform signs, and let $\delta\in(0,1)$. Each of the following four guarantees holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$:

$$\forall g\in\mathcal G,\qquad Pg\le P_mg+2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\forall g\in\mathcal G,\qquad Pg\le P_mg+2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|Pg-P_mg|\le2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|Pg-P_mg|\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\delta)}{2m}}.$$

The four guarantees are separate probability statements. The choice axiom is used through the bounded-differences theorem.

lem-contrastive-uniform-generalization.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the one-negative latent-class model, fix $R>0$, a source loss $\ell\in\{\ell_{\rm h},\ell_{\rm log}\}$, a sample size $M\ge1$, and a sample $S$ of $M$ IID triplets. Assume the loss risks and all sample, independent-copy, and sign suprema below are measurable. Let $B_{\ell,R}=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$ and define

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}},\qquad 0<\delta<1.$$

With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad |L_{\rm un}(f)-\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)|\le\Gamma_M(S,\delta).$$

Here $\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)$ is the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity of the three embeddings in each triplet.

lem-contrastive-class-collision-deviatio.interface:
## Statement

In the one-negative latent-class model, for every bounded representation $f$ and either source loss, the population contrastive loss decomposes as

$$L_{\rm un}(f)=\tau L^=_{\rm un}(f)+(1-\tau)L^\ne_{\rm un}(f).$$

If $\tau>0$, the same-class conditional loss obeys

$$1\le L^=_{\rm un}(f)\le1+c_0s(f),\qquad c_0:=\sqrt2\,L_0,$$

where $L_0$ is the common Lipschitz constant of the hinge and logistic losses. If $\tau=0$, then $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ and the model's convention is $s(f)=0$.

lem-contrastive-empirical-minimizer-exce.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the one-negative uniform-generalization lemma for a sample $S$ of size $M$. Let $\widehat f$ be a measurable random representation such that, almost surely, $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)+\eta$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$, where $\eta\ge0$. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le L_{\rm un}(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)+\eta,$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. The case $\eta=0$ includes any attained measurable empirical minimizer; the statement does not assert that such a selector exists.

lem-mean-classifier-loss-from-contrastiv.interface:
## Statement

Let $C_+,C_-$ be independent with law $\rho$, conditioned on $C_+\ne C_-$, let $X,X^+$ be independent with law $D_{C_+}$, and let $X^-$ be independent with law $D_{C_-}$. For every measurable bounded representation $f$ and either source hinge or logistic loss, the average binary-task mean-classifier risk satisfies

$$L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)\le L^\ne_{\rm un}(f).$$

Here each binary task uses a uniform label from its two classes, and $L^\ne_{\rm un}$ is the contrastive loss conditional on different positive and negative classes.

thm-contrastive-representation-transfer-.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Fix either source hinge or logistic loss and a sample size $M\ge1$. Suppose all risks and suprema in the uniform-generalization statement are measurable and that a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ exists, meaning $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the IID triplet sample,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le\frac{L_{\rm un}(f)-\tau+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau},$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. This is a guarantee for the average binary task with a uniform label and the class-mean linear classifier.

lem-subgaussian-contrastive-margin-compa.interface:
## Statement

In the one-negative latent-class model, fix a bounded representation $f$ with $\sup_x\|f(x)\|_2\le R$, where $R>0$. Use the hinge loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$. Suppose that for every class $c$, the centered vector $f(X)-\mu_c$, for $X\sim D_c$, is sub-Gaussian in every direction with proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, define

$$\gamma:=\begin{cases}1+2R\sigma\sqrt{2\ln R+\ln(3/\epsilon)},&R\ge1,\\1+2R\sigma\sqrt{\ln(3/\epsilon)},&0<R<1.\end{cases}$$

Then the contrastive risk conditioned on distinct positive and negative classes satisfies

$$L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)\le\gamma L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)+\epsilon.$$

This comparison is for the hinge contrastive loss and its scaled hinge mean-classifier risk.

thm-contrastive-representation-transfer-.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Fix either source hinge or logistic loss, $M\ge1$, and a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ satisfying $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely, under the measurability hypotheses of the uniform-generalization result. For each comparator $f\in\mathcal F$ and every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the IID triplet sample,

$$L_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)+\frac{\sqrt2L_0\tau s(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau},$$

where $L_{\rm sup}$ is the infimum of the average binary-task risk over all linear classifiers, $s(f)$ is the within-class covariance deviation, and

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. The event is simultaneous for all comparators.

cor-subgaussian-contrastive-representati.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Use the source hinge loss for both contrastive training and the binary mean-classifier task. Fix $M\ge1$, a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ satisfying $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely, $0<\delta<1$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Let $f\in\mathcal F$ be any comparator whose centered class-conditional representation vectors are sub-Gaussian in every direction with common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$. Define

$$\gamma:=\begin{cases}1+2R\sigma\sqrt{2\ln R+\ln(3/\epsilon)},&R\ge1,\\1+2R\sigma\sqrt{\ln(3/\epsilon)},&0<R<1.\end{cases}$$

Under the risk and supremum measurability hypotheses, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$L_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le\gamma L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)+\epsilon+\frac{\sqrt2L_0\tau s(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau}.$$

The uniform-deviation quantity is

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell_{\rm h},R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}},$$

where $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ is the average task risk of the class-mean weight $w_\mu$ using the scaled hinge loss $(1-Yw_\mu^\top f(X)/\gamma)_+$. The logistic transfer theorems remain separate; the source margin comparison does not supply their logistic analogue.

def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-.interface:
## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

def-continuous-time-stopping-time.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

## Source notes

Durrett, Section 7.3, and Sousi, Section 6.4, define stopping times by
$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ and record the strict-test form for
right-continuous filtrations. The stopped sigma-algebra convention is fixed
here because the strong Markov theorem and the dyadic ceiling argument both
consume the containment $\mathcal F_\tau\subseteq\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$ for
$\tau_n\downarrow\tau$.

def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-it.interface:
## Definition

Fix processes $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ and $Y=(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$ of real random
variables on one probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$: for every
$\omega$ in a measurable event of probability one the paths $t\mapsto X_t$
and $t\mapsto Y_t$ are continuous on $[0,\infty)$
[[def-continuity-real]]. Fix $T>0$ and a deterministic partition sequence
$(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. For each $n$ write
$\pi_n=(m_n,s^{(n)})$ and form the two families of **cross-increment partial
sums**
$$S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t):=\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le m_n\\s^{(n)}_k\le t}}\bigl(X_{s^{(n)}_k}-X_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s^{(n)}_k}-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr),$$
$$S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)+\bigl(X_t-X_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_t-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\quad(k(t)<m_n),$$
with $S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(T):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(T)$ and $k(t)$ the largest
index in $\{0,\ldots,m_n\}$ with $s^{(n)}_{k(t)}\le t$; these are the cross sums corresponding to the
two conventions of
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]] specialized to the pair
$(X,Y)$, and both are $0$ at $t=0$.

All suprema in probability statements below use measurable versions. For
any finite collection of the processes involved, including a candidate limit,
intersect their measurable probability-one continuity events and set all of
them to zero off that intersection. These representatives have everywhere
continuous paths and retain measurable fixed-time values. The partial-sum
paths are continuous; the step-sum paths are right-continuous on $[0,T)$
with the specified value at $T$. Their uniform distances from a continuous
candidate therefore equal suprema over $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,T])\cup\{T\}$,
which are finite measurable random variables. Another such normalization
agrees on a measurable probability-one event and gives the same probability
limits. Here indistinguishability means agreement at every time on a
measurable probability-one event. No completeness or adaptedness is needed
for this convention.

1. **Existence and value of the covariation.** We say that the **quadratic
   covariation $[X,Y]$ exists on $[0,T]$** when there is a real process
   $t\mapsto[X,Y]_t$ of real random variables with almost-sure continuous
   paths on $[0,T]$ such that for *every* deterministic partition
   sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$ both families
   converge to it uniformly in probability on $[0,T]$:
   $$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0, \qquad \sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0,$$
   the convergence being convergence in probability
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. The two displayed requirements are part
   of one condition: the same process $[X,Y]$ must arise for every admissible
   sequence and for both conventions. When the condition holds we call
   $[X,Y]_t$ the **quadratic covariation of $X$ and $Y$ at time $t$**, and we
   write $[X]:=[X,X]$ and call it the **quadratic variation of $X$**. For two candidate limits $U,V$, fix a deterministic dyadic partition
   sequence. The triangle inequality bounds $\sup_t|U_t-V_t|$ by the sum
   of their uniform errors against its partial sums. For each
   $\varepsilon>0$ the probability that this supremum exceeds
   $\varepsilon$ is at most the sum of the two error probabilities at
   $\varepsilon/2$, and hence is zero. Taking $\varepsilon=1/j$,
   $j\ge1$, proves uniqueness on one measurable probability-one event; the definition is applied
   separately on each finite horizon, and when the covariations on all
   horizons are compatible we write the resulting process on $[0,\infty)$
   again as $[X,Y]$.

2. **Symmetry and polarization.** Exchanging the two factors does not change
   the definition, so $[X,Y]=[Y,X]$ whenever either side exists. The
   identities
   $$[X+Y]=[X]+2[X,Y]+[Y],\qquad [X-Y]=[X]-2[X,Y]+[Y]$$
   hold on the domain where all covariations appearing in them exist: the
   cross-increment sums are bilinear in the pair, so the displayed identities
