Let $d,q\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a sigma-finite measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$, let $\pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $(\rho,u^c)$ be a conditional probability-density path and conditional velocity field relative to $(\lambda,\pi)$. Set
$$p_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1),\qquad J_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1).$$
Assume $0<p_t(x)<\infty$ and $J_t(x)$ is finite on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d$, and define $u^m_t(x):=J_t(x)/p_t(x)$. Suppose the conditional continuity equation holds on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, and for every compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ there is a nonnegative $G_K\in L^1(\pi)$ that bounds on $K$, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, the absolute values of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, $\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, each component of $\rho_tu^c_t$, and each corresponding spatial flux derivative.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:\,[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and continuously differentiable in $\theta$, with jointly measurable parameter derivative. Define
$$\mathcal L_C(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} \rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)\,dt,$$
and
$$\mathcal L_M(\theta):=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} p_t(x)\|v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\lambda(dx)\,dt.$$
Assume $\mathcal L_C(\theta)$ and $\mathcal L_M(\theta)$ are finite for every $\theta\in\Theta$, and define
$$C:=\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathbb R^d} \rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)\,dt,$$
and assume $C<\infty$. For every compact $H\subset\Theta$ and coordinate $j$, suppose there are nonnegative integrable majorants $G^C_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)\,\pi(dx_1)$ and $G^M_{H,j}$ on $dt\,\lambda(dx)$ such that for every $\theta\in H$, outside fixed null sets,
$$2\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^c_t(x\mid x_1)\right\rangle\right|\le G^C_{H,j}(t,x,x_1),$$
and
$$2p_t(x)\left|\left\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-u^m_t(x)\right\rangle\right|\le G^M_{H,j}(t,x).$$
Then both objectives are finite and continuously differentiable on $\Theta$, and $\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+C$. In particular, $C$ is independent of $\theta$ and $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$. Under the stated local domination, $(p,u^m)$ also satisfies the marginal continuity equation on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. Uniform boundedness of $u^c,u^m,v,D_\theta v$ on compact parameter neighborhoods is a sufficient special case of the integrability and derivative-majorant assumptions above.

def-neural-ode.interface:
## Definition

Let $d,q\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$. For a parameter $\theta\in\Theta$, write $v_\theta(t,z):=v(t,z,\theta)$. A **parameterized neural ordinary differential equation**, or **neural ODE**, on $I$ is the initial-value problem

$$\dot z(t)=v_\theta(t,z(t)),\qquad z(s)=z_s,$$

where $s\in I$ and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$. A trajectory on an interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$ is a differentiable function $z:J\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying both displayed conditions. Here $v_\theta$ is the state-velocity field. The term names this parameterized vector-field model and imposes no particular neural-network architecture. This definition alone asserts neither solution existence beyond its stated interval nor numerical accuracy.

thm-neural-ode-global-smooth-flow.interface:
## Statement

Let $T>0$, let $d,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $v:I\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly $C^\infty$. For every compact $K\subseteq\Theta$, suppose there are constants $L_K,M_K\ge0$ such that, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\theta\in K$, and $z,w\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|v(t,z,\theta)-v(t,w,\theta)\|_2\le L_K\|z-w\|_2,\qquad \|v(t,0,\theta)\|_2\le M_K.$$

Then for each $\theta\in\Theta$, $s,t\in[0,T]$, and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$, the neural ODE has a unique solution on all of $[0,T]$. Write $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ for its value at time $t$. For each fixed $s,t$, the map $(z_s,\theta)\mapsto\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ is locally $C^\infty$. For each fixed $\theta$, $\Phi^\theta_{t,s}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi^\theta_{s,t}$. Its state Jacobian $J_{t,s}:=D_{z_s}\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s)$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}J_{t,s}=D_zv(t,\Phi^\theta_{t,s}(z_s),\theta)J_{t,s},\qquad J_{s,s}=I_d.$$

Time derivatives at $0$ and $T$ are one-sided.

thm-gaussian-conditional-optimal-transpo.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and choose $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let $Z$ have the standard multivariate normal law $N_d(0,I_d)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, define
$$\mu_t(x_1):=t x_1,\qquad \sigma_t:=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad \psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t z+\mu_t(x_1),$$
and let $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ be the law of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$. Then $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian probability path with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, and its Lebesgue density is
$$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$
A conditional velocity field for this path is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)+x_1.$$
For each endpoint $x_1$, these densities and fields form a conditional path in the probability-path definition; hence they can be mixed against any Borel endpoint law. At $t=0$ the law is $N_d(0,I_d)$, and at $t=1$ it is the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$, a Gaussian with mean $x_1$ and covariance $\sigma_{\min}^2I_d$. The affine endpoint map $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$ is optimal for squared Euclidean cost between these two laws: every coupling has cost at least
$$\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2,$$
and the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains this value.

thm-extreme-value-metric.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-ra.interface:
## Definition

Let $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ be a feature-response measurable
space, let $m\ge0$, and put $n=m+1$. A **split score rule** is a jointly
measurable map $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, where $H$ is a
training statistic with values in the specified measurable rule space
$(\mathcal H,\mathscr H)$. The measurable-statistic convention is that of
[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Once $H=h$ is fixed, calibration and test
scores are $R_i=s(h,Z_i)$; the rule does not change when it scores the
calibration or test example.

A **full score assignment** of length $n$ is a measurable map
$A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n):\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ that is
permutation-equivariant:
$$A(\tau_\pi z)=\tau_\pi A(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z^n\text{ and permutation }\pi.$$
For a candidate response $y$, append $(x,y)$ as the $n$th example and write
$R_i(y)=A_i(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,(x,y))$ and $r=R_n(y)$.

For either a split score vector or a full augmented score vector, the
**nonrandomized upper-rank p-value** of the candidate is
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$
An optional **tie-randomized rank p-value** is defined when a supplied random
variable $U$ has Lebesgue probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of the
data and training information:
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)>r\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)=r\}\bigr)}{m+1}.$$
The added $1$ counts the candidate itself in its tie group. A single such $U$
is shared across a candidate scan. This is an explicit randomization; the
general Markov-kernel definition of a randomized procedure
[[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]] does not assert that arbitrary
kernels have a random-seed representation.

Here “uniform on $[0,1]$” means $\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$.

Smaller scores are treated as more conforming. The rank formula counts all
ties conservatively in the nonrandomized version; the randomized formula
spreads the candidate uniformly over its entire tie block.

For a split candidate scan at a fixed feature value $x$, the notation in
these formulas is $R_i(y)=s(h,Z_i)$ for $1\le i\le m$ and
$R_n(y)=s(h,(x,y))$, with $r=R_n(y)$. Thus the calibration scores do not
depend on $y$, and the candidate is scored by the same fixed rule.

def-statistic-and-estimator.interface:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

alg-split-conformal-prediction-set.interface:
## Definition

Let $m\ge0$ calibration examples $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ be scored by one fixed,
measurable score rule $s_H$ obtained from the training statistic $H$, and let
$0<\alpha<1$. Set
$$n=m+1,\qquad k=\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil.$$
Compute $R_i=s_H(Z_i)$ for $1\le i\le m$. Sort calibration observations by
the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$, so ties are broken by the fixed index order. If
$k\le m$, let $q$ be the score component of the $k$th ordered pair; if
$k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a feature value $x$, return
$$C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s_H(x,y)\le q\}.$$

The optional tie-randomized version uses one independent $U$ with Lebesgue
probability law on $[0,1]$, shared across the candidate scan, and returns
$$C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\},$$
where $p_U$ is the score-rank formula in
[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]]. The candidate score is
included in its tie group. The score maps must be jointly measurable in the
training, calibration, feature, and response variables; then membership in
each returned set is a measurable event by
[[lem-finite-order-statistic-and-rank-maps-are-measurable]].

lem-finite-order-statistic-and-rank-maps.interface:
## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable space, let $R_1,\ldots,R_m$ be
measurable real-valued functions with $m\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le m$. The
$k$th order statistic $R_{(k)}$ is measurable. For a finite real score vector
$R_1,\ldots,R_n$ and another measurable real-valued function $U$ on the same
space, its upper-rank p-value and tie-randomized rank are measurable.

def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-event.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

def-probability-calibration.interface:
## Definition

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

def-proper-scoring-rule.interface:
## Definition

For an integer $K\ge2$, let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and let $\Delta_K=\{q\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kq_j=1\}$. A finite-label score loss is a function $S:\Delta_K\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty]$ whose section $q\mapsto S(q,j)$ is Borel measurable for every label $j$. If the true label distribution is $p\in\Delta_K$ and the reported forecast is $q\in\Delta_K$, its expected score loss is $\bar S(p,q)=\sum_{j=1}^Kp_jS(q,j)$, where a term with $p_j=0$ contributes zero even when $S(q,j)=+\infty$. The loss is **proper** if $\bar S(p,p)\le\bar S(p,q)$ for every $p,q\in\Delta_K$, and **strictly proper** if equality implies $q=p$. The logarithmic loss is $S_{\log}(q,j)=-\log q_j$, with $-\log0=+\infty$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm; the Brier loss is $S_{\mathrm B}(q,j)=\sum_{i=1}^K(q_i-\mathbf1_{\{i=j\}})^2$.

thm-log-and-brier-strict-propriety.interface:
## Statement

For every $K\ge2$ and $p,q\in\Delta_K$, the logarithmic and Brier losses in the definition of finite-label score loss satisfy $\bar S(p,p)\le\bar S(p,q)$, with equality only when $q=p$. The expected logarithmic loss at the truthful forecast is finite, including when some coordinates of $p$ vanish.

def-top-label-calibration.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $K\ge2$, let
$Y:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have the full power-set sigma-algebra, and let
$G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable random forecast, where
the probability simplex is
$\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}$. Define the predicted label and
top confidence by
$$\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell\},\qquad C=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell.$$
The smallest-index rule resolves ties. The forecast is **top-label calibrated**
if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
Thus, among predictions whose top confidence lies in any specified set of
confidence values, the frequency of a correct top label equals the average
reported top confidence.

alg-validation-temperature-scaling.interface:
## Definition

Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Choose the smallest temperature among the minimizers,
$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

def-binned-expected-calibration-error.interface:
## Definition

Let $K\ge2$ and let $(\widehat p_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a nonempty finite
evaluation sample, where $\widehat p_i\in\Delta_K$ and
$y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. For each $i$, let
$\widehat y_i=\min\arg\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$,
$c_i=\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$, and
$a_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\widehat y_i=y_i\}}$. Fix before evaluating the sample a
finite Borel partition $(B_1,\ldots,B_M)$ of $[0,1]$. For
$I_b=\{i:c_i\in B_b\}$ and $n_b=|I_b|>0$, define
$$\operatorname{acc}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}a_i,\qquad \operatorname{conf}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}c_i.$$
The **binned expected calibration error** and **binned maximum calibration
error** for this sample and partition are
$$\operatorname{ECE}_{(B_b)}=\sum_{b:n_b>0}\frac{n_b}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|,\qquad \operatorname{MCE}_{(B_b)}=\max_{b:n_b>0}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|.$$
These are finite-sample, bin-dependent summaries, not the population expected
calibration error. They compare observed top-label accuracy with average
confidence within bins; log loss and Brier loss instead score probability
forecasts directly and are strictly proper.

thm-positive-temperature-scaling-preserv.interface:
## Statement

Let $K\ge2$, let $z\in\mathbb R^K$, and let $T>0$. Define
$$p_j(T)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K).$$
Then $p(T)$ lies in the interior of $\Delta_K$ and
$\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}p_j(T)
=\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}z_j$.
For the finite validation inputs and candidate temperatures specified in the
validation temperature-scaling algorithm, every validation loss is finite and
the stated smallest-minimizer rule returns a unique candidate.

alg-split-conformal-set-for-classificati.interface:
## Definition

Let $K\ge2$, let the feature space be a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and
let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with all subsets measurable.
Let $H$ be a training statistic valued in a measurable rule space $\mathcal H$,
and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable score rule. The rule is fixed after training and is used
unchanged on calibration and test examples. Given $m\ge0$ calibration examples
$(X_i,Y_i)$ and $0<\alpha<1$, compute
$$R_i=s(H,X_i,Y_i),\qquad k=\left\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil.$$
If $k\le m$, sort the calibration scores by the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$ and let
$q$ be the score value at position $k$. If $k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a
feature value $x$, return the prediction set
$$
C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s(H,x,y)\le q\}.
$$
For the optional tie-randomized version, use one random variable $U$ that is
uniform on $[0,1]$ and independent of the training information and all
calibration and test examples, shared across the candidate-label scan. For
$r_y=s(H,x,y)$, define
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i>r_y\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i=r_y\}\bigr)}{m+1},\qquad C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\}.$$
The candidate is included in its own tie group. The algorithm defines these
sets; any coverage claim requires separate distributional hypotheses.

thm-split-conformal-marginal-coverage.interface:
## Statement

Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m+1$, be random elements of one measurable
example space $(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$, and let $\mathcal T$ be the training
sigma-field. Suppose the tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})$ has a regular
conditional distribution $Q_\omega$ given $\mathcal T$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], whose sections have joint laws
invariant under every coordinate permutation, as in
[[def-exchangeable-random-elements]], for almost every $\omega$. Let $H$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable
training statistic, and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable split score rule. Use the split set in
[[alg-split-conformal-prediction-set]] at $0<\alpha<1$. Then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
If the tie-randomized set $C_U$ is used with one $U$ of Lebesgue probability
law on $[0,1]$ independent of $\mathcal T\vee\sigma(Z)$, then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C_U(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}=1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
In either case, integration over the training sigma-field gives the same
marginal lower bound or exact marginal coverage.

def-regular-conditional-distribution.interface:
## Definition

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

def-exchangeable-random-elements.interface:
## Definition

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be random elements, $n\ge1$, of one measurable space
$(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$. Their tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ is a random element
of $(\mathcal Z^n,\mathscr Z^{\otimes n})$ by
[[lem-coordinate-maps-and-permutations-are-measurable-on-finite-products]],
and its law is the pushforward probability measure from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For a permutation $\pi$ of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\tau_\pi(z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$. The tuple is
**exchangeable** if
$$\mathbb P_Z\circ\tau_\pi^{-1}=\mathbb P_Z\qquad\text{for every permutation }\pi.$$

This is invariance of the joint law, not an assertion of independence or identical marginal construction by independent sampling. The coordinate maps $\tau_\pi$ are measurable by the cited finite-product lemma.

def-online-decision-protocol.interface:
## Definition

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

def-adversary-and-feedback-model.interface:
## Definition

In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigm.interface:
## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

## Source notes

Durrett §4.1, printed pp.205–206; van der Vaart §1.1, Definition 1.1, printed p.1. Integrability is imposed explicitly here.

def-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator.interface:
## Definition

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

alg-hedge.interface:
## Definition

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with $\mathbb P(I_t=i)=x_t(i)$, and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. Every factor $\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))$ is a positive finite real; from the positive finite initial weights it follows by induction that every normalizing denominator is positive and finite. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

alg-exp3.interface:
## Definition

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The output is $(P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widehat Y_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $\widehat S_n$. These operations use exact real arithmetic. The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. It is well-defined by induction: $\widehat S_{0,i}$ is finite; if the previous estimates are finite, every exponential weight is positive and finite, so the finite normalizing sum is positive and finite and $P_{t,i}>0$; then the observed loss estimate and update are finite. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge. Equivalently, since $\widehat S_{t-1,i}=(t-1)-\sum_{s<t}\widehat Y_{s,i}$, subtracting the common constant $t-1$ leaves the same probabilities as weights proportional to $\exp(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\widehat Y_{s,i})$.

lem-bandit-importance-weighted-estimator.interface:
## Statement

In the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition, fix a round $t$ and arm $i$, and write $p=P_{t,i}>0$ and $y=y_{t,i}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i},\qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\frac{y_{t,i}^2}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
With conditional variance defined by $\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}])^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, one also has
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\frac{y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})}{P_{t,i}}.
$$

def-static-dynamic-and-strongly-adaptive.interface:
## Definition

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class only if there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

lem-exponential-dominates-one-plus-x.interface:
## Statement

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

def-contextual-bandit-protocol.interface:
## Definition

Fix integers $n\ge1$, $k>1$, and $M>1$. Write $[r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}$ for a positive integer $r$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\},\qquad \mathcal E=\Delta_k^M.
$$
An oblivious contextual bandit instance consists of reward vectors $x_t\in[0,1]^k$ and advice matrices $E(t)\in\mathcal E$, for $t\in[n]$, all fixed before the learner's private randomization. The matrix $E(t)$ is revealed before the round-$t$ action; its row $E(t)_m=(E(t)_{m,1},\ldots,E(t)_{m,k})$ is expert $m$'s probability distribution over the $k$ actions. The expected reward of expert $m$ on round $t$ is $\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^k E(t)_{m,i}x_{t,i}$.

At round $t$, the learner's pre-action history consists of its earlier actions and observed rewards. Given that history and the revealed advice, it selects a distribution $P_t\in\Delta_k$, draws a measurable finite-valued action $A_t\in[k]$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$. Here $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the pre-action history. For every fixed expert sequence and reward sequence, the **expected regret against the best fixed expert** is
$$
R_n=\mathbb E\left[\max_{m\in[M]}\sum_{t=1}^n\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle-\sum_{t=1}^n X_t\right],
$$
where expectation is over the learner's action draws. The regret random variable is bounded, so this expectation is finite. This protocol makes no stochastic generalization claim and imposes no shared-structure condition on the experts; it does not cover advice or rewards selected in response to the learner's current action.

alg-exp4.interface:
## Definition

Given integers $n\ge1$, $k>1$, $M>1$, a learning rate $\eta>0$, and an instance from the contextual bandit protocol with finite expert advice, initialize $Q_{1,m}=1/M$ for $m\in[M]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Receive the advice matrix $E(t)$, whose $m$th row is $E(t)_m\in\Delta_k$.

2. Form the action distribution
$$
P_{t,i}=\sum_{m=1}^M Q_{t,m}E(t)_{m,i},\qquad i\in[k].
$$

3. Draw a measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$ and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.

4. For each $i\in[k]$, form
$$
\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
When $P_{t,i}=0$, the action $A_t=i$ is impossible; in this case the quotient term is defined to be zero on every possible outcome.

5. For each expert $m\in[M]$, form its estimated reward
$$
\widetilde X_{t,m}=\sum_{i=1}^kE(t)_{m,i}\widehat X_{t,i}
$$
and update the expert distribution by
$$
Q_{t+1,m}=\frac{Q_{t,m}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,m})}{\sum_{r=1}^M Q_{t,r}\exp(\eta\widetilde X_{t,r})}.
$$

The output is $(Q_t,P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widetilde X_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $Q_{n+1}$. All arithmetic is over exact real numbers, and the procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated finite-valued measurable draws. It is well-defined by induction: each row of $E(t)$ is a probability vector and each $Q_t$ is a probability vector, so $P_t\in\Delta_k$; the zero-probability convention and $P_{t,i}>0$ otherwise make every estimate finite; and positive finite exponential weights give a positive finite normalizing denominator and a probability vector $Q_{t+1}$ with all entries positive. This is the $\gamma=0$ Exp4 update; no regret guarantee for bounded-loss Hedge is part of the algorithm.

lem-exp4-unbiased-expert-reward-estimate.interface:
## Statement

In Exp4, at every round $t\in[n]$ and for every expert $m\in[M]$, the expert's estimated reward satisfies
$$
\mathbb E[\widetilde X_{t,m}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\langle E(t)_m,x_t\rangle.
$$
The assertion includes rounds where some actions have zero sampling probability; no componentwise unbiasedness claim is made for an unsupported action.

lem-exp4-weighted-estimated-loss-second-.interface:
## Statement

At every round $t$ in Exp4, define the estimated action loss by $\widehat L_{t,i}=1-\widehat X_{t,i}$ and the estimated loss of expert $m$ by $\widetilde L_{t,m}=1-\widetilde X_{t,m}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E\left[\sum_{m=1}^M Q_{t,m}\widetilde L_{t,m}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal F_{t-1}\right]\le k.
$$
This bound includes actions with zero sampling probability under the zero-quotient convention.

lem-exp4-potential-inequality.interface:
## Statement

For any Exp4 run with learning rate $\eta>0$ and any fixed expert $m^*\in[M]$, define $\widetilde L_{t,m}=1-\widetilde X_{t,m}$. The following pathwise inequality holds for every realized action sequence:
$$
\sum_{t=1}^n\widetilde X_{t,m^*}-\sum_{t=1}^n\sum_{m=1}^M Q_{t,m}\widetilde X_{t,m}\le\frac{\log M}{\eta}+\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=1}^n\sum_{m=1}^M Q_{t,m}\widetilde L_{t,m}^{2}.
$$

lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-u.interface:
## Statement

In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, every $x\ge0$ has a unique $y\ge0$ with
$y^2=x$.

thm-exp4-expected-regret.interface:
## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $k>1$, and $M>1$ be integers. For each $t\in[n]$, let $x_t\in[0,1]^k$ and let $E(t)$ be an $M\times k$ matrix with nonnegative entries whose every row sums to one. Assume the reward vectors and advice matrices are deterministic and fixed before learner randomization, each advice matrix is revealed before its action, and the learner observes only the reward of its sampled action. Run Exp4 with
$$
\eta=\sqrt{\frac{2\log M}{nk}},
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and the square root is the nonnegative real root. Define expected regret against the best fixed expert by
$$
R_n=\mathbb E\left[\max_{m\in[M]}\sum_{t=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k E(t)_{m,i}x_{t,i}-\sum_{t=1}^n X_t\right],\qquad [M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}.
$$
Then
$$
R_n\le\sqrt{2nk\log M}.
$$

def-finite-markov-decision-process.interface:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

def-cartesian-product.interface:
## Definition

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. By
[[lem-ordered-pairs-lie-in-the-double-power-set]] every ordered pair $(a,b)$ with
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$ is an element of $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B))$, so
[[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]] applied inside that set produces the
**Cartesian product**

$$A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}.$$

Its elements are exactly the ordered pairs $(a,b)$ ([[def-ordered-pair]]) with
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$: no such pair is lost, because each such pair lies in
the ambient set being separated. Thus $z \in A \times B$ holds if and only if
$z = (a,b)$ for some $a \in A$ and some $b \in B$.

## Remarks

- **Why the ambient set is needed.** "The set of all ordered pairs with first
  coordinate in $A$ and second in $B$" is a class abbreviation, and no axiom
  turns a class abbreviation into a set on its own. The double power set is what
  supplies a set to separate inside, so the product costs
  [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-of-union]] as well as Separation;
  [[rem-which-axiom-each-construction-uses]] keeps the account.

- **Products of nonempty sets.** Whether a product of *two* nonempty sets is
  nonempty is settled here, by exhibiting the pair
  ([[prop-cartesian-products-and-set-operations]]). The corresponding question
  for a product of an arbitrary indexed family of nonempty sets is not settled by
  the axioms on this page: it is one formulation of the Axiom of Choice, stated
  at [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

def-pac-mdp-bounded-reward-model.interface:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite set for each $s\in S$, and let $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number. Put $S_0=|S|$ and $A_0=\max_{s\in S}|A(s)|$. Fix a discount $0\le\gamma<1$. Give $S$ and $D$ their discrete sigma-algebras and give $[0,1]$ its Borel sigma-algebra. A **bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process** is a probability kernel $K$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$. At pair $(s,a)$, $K(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is the joint law of the next state and the reward; these two coordinates need not be independent. Define the state-transition probabilities and expected rewards by

$$P(s'\mid s,a)=K(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,K(ds',d\rho\mid s,a).$$

A **history-dependent behavior** is a sequence of probability kernels from observed-history spaces $H_t$ to the finite action alphabet $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$, assigning probability zero to actions outside $A(s_t)$ at every history ending in state $s_t$. Here $H_t$ consists of histories $(s_0,a_0,R_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},R_t,s_t)$, with discrete sigma-algebras on finite state/action coordinates and the Borel sigma-algebra on each reward coordinate; it has the resulting finite-product sigma-algebra. A **stationary Markov policy** assigns one distribution on $A(s)$ to each state, independently of earlier history. During interaction, after choosing $a_t$ in state $s_t$, the next pair $(s_{t+1},R_{t+1})$ is drawn from $K(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)$.

thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-mar.interface:
## Statement

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

thm-sequential-suprema-infima-limsup-lim.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

thm-geometric-series.interface:
## Statement

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

thm-reals-cauchy-complete.interface:
## Statement

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

def-countable.interface:
## Definition

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

## Remarks

- **Convention: in this library "countable" alone always means "at most
  countable"**, so a finite set is countable. This is the convention of Halmos
  and of Tao, and it is the one that makes the theorems on this page read
  cleanly: subsets, products and unions of countable sets are countable, with no
  finite/infinite case split in the statement. The competing convention, used by
  Rudin among others, reserves "countable" for "countably infinite" and says
  "at most countable" for the disjunction. Under that convention every statement
  below still holds after replacing "countable" with "at most countable", but
  several would become false as literally written. Where the distinction
  matters, the long forms "countably infinite" and "at most countable" are used
  in full, and "uncountable" always means "not at most countable", on which the
  two conventions agree.

- **The three classes are exhaustive by construction**: every set is finite,
  countably infinite, or uncountable, since "uncountable" is defined as the
  negation of the disjunction. That they are also mutually exclusive, that is,
  that no set is both finite and countably infinite, is a genuine theorem
  amounting to $\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and it is
  proved immediately above as claim 4 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So a countably
  infinite set is never finite, and "$A$ is infinite", meaning not finite, is
  implied by $A \approx \mathbb{N}$. The same lemma pins down finiteness itself:
  by its claim 3 a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number, so
  the number of elements of a finite set is well defined, and by its claim 5 no
  finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself.

- **What the exclusivity is and is not used for below.** Nothing on this page
  needs it in order to run: the infinitude of $\mathbb{Q}$, for instance, is
  obtained by exhibiting a bijection $\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ directly
  ([[thm-rationals-countable]]) rather than by ruling out finiteness. It is used
  when the continuum hypothesis is instantiated at $\mathbb{N}$
  ([[rem-continuum-hypothesis]]), where $\mathbb{N}$ must be infinite as a fact
  rather than as a convention.

- **$0$ and the empty set.** $0 = \varnothing$, and $A \approx 0$ holds exactly
  when $A = \varnothing$, so the empty set is finite. This matters in the proofs
  below, where the empty case is always separated out: a surjection
  $\mathbb{N} \to A$ cannot exist when $A = \varnothing$, which is why
  [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]] assumes $A$ nonempty.

- **Countability is a property of a set alone**, not of a set with structure. In
  particular $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable while carrying a dense order, and
  $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable; neither statement says anything on its own about
  the order or the arithmetic those sets carry.

lem-triangle-inequality-finite.interface:
## Statement

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the absolute value as in
[[def-abs-value]]. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

lem-finite-choice.interface:
## Statement

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F$ be a function with domain $n$ all of whose
values are nonempty sets. Then the family of its values,
$\mathcal{F} = F[n] = \{\, F(i) : i \in n \,\}$, has a choice function
([[def-choice-function]]).

This is a theorem of ZF: its proof uses no form of the Axiom of Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$. The
natural number $n$ serves as the index set in the von Neumann sense,
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "$F$ has domain $n$"
says precisely that the members of $\mathcal{F}$ are listed as
$F(0), \dots, F(n-1)$. The listing need not be injective, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the
set of values, so repetitions are harmless and are not counted.

The displayed statement and its proof use only a natural-number-indexed
function. They do not identify an arbitrary finite family with a particular
enumeration.

lem-conditional-hoeffding-bound-for-boun.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $D\in L^1$ satisfy $\mathbb E[D\mid\mathcal G]=0$ almost surely. Let $A,B$ be finite $\mathcal G$-measurable random variables such that $A\le D\le B$ and $B-A\le c$ almost surely for a deterministic $c\ge0$. Then for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D}\mid\mathcal G]\le e^{\lambda^2c^2/8}\quad\text{a.s.}$$

thm-azuma-hoeffding-inequality.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

thm-finite-union-bound.interface:
## Statement

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

thm-pac-mdp-value-functions.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In every bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, and $0\le\gamma<1$, the trajectory law of every history-dependent behavior from every starting state exists. Its discounted return is measurable, integrable, and between $0$ and $1/(1-\gamma)$. For each stationary policy $\pi$, its value $V^\pi$ satisfies its Bellman equation. The optimality operator

$$T^*V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

is a $\gamma$ contraction in the supremum norm, meaning $\|T^*V-T^*W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty$ for all $V,W:S\to\mathbb R$, where $\|V\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|V(s)|$, and has a unique fixed point $V^*$. This fixed point is the supremum of the values of all history-dependent behaviors and is attained by a deterministic stationary greedy policy. The optimal action value is

$$Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V^*(s'),$$

and $V^*(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q^*(s,a)$ with $Q^*(s,a)\ge0$.

def-admissible-mdp-heuristic.interface:
## Definition

For a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an **admissible upper heuristic** is a function $U:D\to[0,V_0]$ such that $Q^*(s,a)\le U(s,a)$ for every admissible pair and a supplied scalar satisfies $0\le V_0\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. Define the effective reward-scale cap $V_{\max}=\max\{1,V_0\}$. Then $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The floor at $1$ is part of this convention because an observed reward can lie anywhere in $[0,1]$, even when the heuristic values are all smaller than $1$.

alg-q-learning.interface:
## Definition

For a finite discounted MDP with $0\le\gamma<1$, maintain an action-value table $Q_n\in\mathbb R^D$. At time $n$, a behavior rule selects the current pair $(S_n,A_n)$ and the process returns reward $R_{n+1}$ and next state $S_{n+1}$. Compute

$$
\delta_n=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in A(S_{n+1})}Q_n(S_{n+1},b)-Q_n(S_n,A_n),
$$

and update only the visited coordinate:

$$
Q_{n+1}(S_n,A_n)=Q_n(S_n,A_n)+\alpha_n(S_n,A_n)\delta_n.
$$

All other coordinates remain unchanged. The update target uses the greedy maximum even when the behavior rule is exploratory, so the algorithm is off-policy and uses no importance-sampling ratio. The update rule by itself asserts no convergence guarantee.

def-pac-mdp-sample-complexity.interface:
## Definition

Assume AC, fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an initial state, and a learning algorithm whose behavior is a history-dependent policy. At time $t\ge1$, let $h_t$ be the observed history ending at state $s_t$. The continuation behavior $A_t$ is the tail of the algorithm's action kernels after $h_t$, and $V^{A_t}(h_t)$ is the expected discounted return of the continuation process generated from that fixed history by those tail kernels. Set $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_{s\in S}|A(s)|$.
For $\epsilon\ge0$, the $\epsilon$-bad-step count is
$$N_\epsilon=\#\{t\ge1:V^{A_t}(h_t)<V^*(s_t)-\epsilon\},$$
where the count may be infinite. For $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\delta<1$, a PAC-MDP bound is a specified finite function $B(S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$ such that, for every MDP with these finite state/action sizes and every initial state, $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le B(S,A,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma))\ge1-\delta$. This definition does not require the bad steps to precede a permanent stopping time.

def-pac-mdp-known-state-action-mdp.interface:
## Definition

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP with discount $\gamma$, let $K\subseteq D$ be a set of known state-action pairs, and let $q:D\to[0,V_{\max}]$ with $V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The **known-state/action MDP** $M_K(q)$ agrees with $M$ on every pair in $K$. For each pair $(s,a)\notin K$, add a distinct absorbing state $\bot_{s,a}$ with one admissible action. The unknown pair transitions deterministically to $\bot_{s,a}$ and gives deterministic reward $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)$; the sink action self-loops with the same deterministic reward $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)$. These rewards lie in $[0,1]$. The sink state's value is $q(s,a)$, so the unknown pair's Bellman backup is exactly $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)+\gamma q(s,a)=q(s,a)$, independent of the value function on the original states.

alg-r-max.interface:
## Definition

Input a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP interaction, its discount $0\le\gamma<1$, an admissible upper heuristic $U$ with cap $V_{\max}$, an integer sample threshold $m\ge1$, a value-iteration error tolerance $0<\beta<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and a fixed total order on each finite action set. Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm. Initialize each pair as unknown, set $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, and give each pair an empty list of observed rewards and next states. At each time $t$, choose a maximizing action in the current state using the fixed tie order, take it, and observe reward $R_{t+1}$ and next state $S_{t+1}$. If the pair is unknown, append this observation until its list has length $m$. When it reaches $m$, mark the pair known, set its empirical reward to the sample mean and its empirical transition law to the sample frequencies, and rebuild all action values by $L$ sweeps from $Q_0(s,a)=0$ of the operator
$$H_KQ(s,a)=\begin{cases}\widehat r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}\widehat P(s'\mid s,a)\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b),&(s,a)\in K,\\ U(s,a),&(s,a)\notin K,\end{cases}$$
where $K$ is the current known set and
$$L=\max\!\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1/[\beta(1-\gamma)])}{1-\gamma}\right\rceil\right\}.$$
Pairs and their samples are never removed from $K$ or discarded. The algorithm specifies no computational-time bound.

lem-pac-mdp-adaptive-sample-concentratio.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC and fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP with state set $S$. For each admissible pair $(s,a)$, let $(S'_i,R_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an independent potential stream with common joint law $K(\cdot\mid s,a)$; an interaction reveals the next unused sample from that pair's stream only when the pair is visited. This construction has the same finite-trajectory law as interaction with the MDP under any history-dependent behavior. For a fixed pair and $m\ge1$, its reward samples satisfy
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m R_i-r(s,a)\right|>x\right)\le 2e^{-2mx^2}\qquad(x>0).$$
If $\widehat P_m$ is the empirical distribution of $S'_1,\ldots,S'_m$ and $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is the true next-state marginal, then
$$\mathbb E\|\widehat P_m-P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le\sqrt{\frac{|S|}{m}},\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\|\widehat P_m-P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1>\sqrt{\frac{|S|}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{m}}\right)\le\delta\quad(0<\delta<1),$$
where $\|q\|_1=\sum_{s'\in S}|q(s')|$ and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.
More generally, for a filtration $(\mathcal F_i)_{i=0}^m$, if $Y_i$ is $\mathcal F_i$-measurable, $0\le Y_i\le B$, and $\mu_i=\mathbb E[Y_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]$, then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i-\mu_i)\right|\ge mx\right)\le2e^{-2mx^2/B^2}\qquad(B>0,\ x>0).$$
No independence between reward and next state within a single transition is assumed. The confidence bounds are for a fixed deterministic sample size or a fixed-size batch; this item makes no uniform confidence claim at a data-dependent sample count. At a finite history-dependent visit count, the next fixed number of unused potential outcomes still has its conditional iid law.

lem-pac-mdp-value-simulation.interface:
## Statement

Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be bounded-reward finite discounted MDPs on the same finite state set $S$ and the same admissible action sets, with common discount $0\le\gamma<1$. Write $r_i,P_i,V_i^\pi,V_i^*$ for their mean rewards, transition laws, stationary-policy values, and optimal values. Suppose $0\le V_i^\pi(s),V_i^*(s)\le V$ for every state, model index $i$, and stationary policy $\pi$, and that for every admissible pair
$$|r_1(s,a)-r_2(s,a)|\le\alpha,\qquad \|P_1(\cdot\mid s,a)-P_2(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le\beta.$$
For finite vectors, $\|v\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|v(s)|$ and $\|p\|_1=\sum_{s\in S}|p(s)|$.
Then every common stationary policy and the optimal values satisfy
$$\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty\le\frac{\alpha+\gamma V\beta}{1-\gamma},\qquad \|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty\le\frac{\alpha+\gamma V\beta}{1-\gamma}.$$
There is also a trap-model form that does not assume a tight cap for the second model: for $W>0$, suppose all stationary-policy and optimal values in $M_1$ are at most $2W$, all rewards in $M_2$ lie in $[0,1]$, and $\gamma\beta\le(1-\gamma)/2$. Then every common stationary policy and the optimal values satisfy
$$\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty\le\frac{2(\alpha+2\gamma W\beta)}{1-\gamma},\qquad \|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty\le\frac{2(\alpha+2\gamma W\beta)}{1-\gamma}.$$

alg-delayed-q-learning.interface:
## Definition

Input a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP interaction, its discount $0\le\gamma<1$, an admissible upper heuristic $U$ with cap $V_{\max}$, an integer batch size $m\ge1$, a bonus $0<\epsilon_1<1$, and a fixed total order on each action set. Initialize $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, batch sum $B(s,a)=0$, sample count $\ell(s,a)=0$, batch start $b(s,a)=0$, learning flag $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$, and global last-update time $t^*=0$. At time $t$, in state $s$, choose an action maximizing $Q(s,\cdot)$ under the fixed tie order, then observe reward $r$ and next state $s'$. If $b(s,a)\le t^*$, set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$. If $L(s,a)$ is true, set $b(s,a)=t$ when $\ell(s,a)=0$, increment $\ell(s,a)$ by one, and add $r+\gamma\max_{c\in A(s')}Q(s',c)$ to $B(s,a)$. When $\ell(s,a)=m$, set $\bar B=B(s,a)/m$. If $Q(s,a)-\bar B\ge2\epsilon_1$, replace $Q(s,a)$ by $\bar B+\epsilon_1$ and set $t^*=t$. Otherwise set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{false}$ exactly when $b(s,a)>t^*$. In every case reset $B(s,a)=0$ and $\ell(s,a)=0$ after the batch; leave all other entries unchanged.

lem-r-max-empirical-model-accuracy.interface:
## Statement

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, let $0<\eta<V_{\max}/4$ and $0<\delta<1$, and let $U,V_{\max}$ be an admissible heuristic with $V_{\max}=\max\{1,V_0\}$. Put
$$b=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{64V_{\max}},\quad L_0=\ln\frac{8SA}{\delta},\quad m=\left\lceil\frac{8(S+L_0)}{b^2}\right\rceil,\quad \beta=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
where $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$. Run R-MAX with this sample threshold and approximation tolerance. For $K_t$ the current known set, let $\widehat M_{K_t}$ use its empirical laws on $K_t$ and the heuristic absorbing states elsewhere, and let $M_{K_t}=M_{K_t}(U)$ use the true laws on $K_t$. Define $E_\eta=\{(s,a):U(s,a)\ge V^*(s)-\eta\}$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously at all times: every stationary-policy value in $\widehat M_{K_t}$ differs from its value in $M_{K_t}$ by at most $\eta/8$; the current action values satisfy $\|Q_t-Q^*_{\widehat M_{K_t}}\|_\infty\le\beta$ and $0\le Q_t(s,a)\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$; the greedy value obeys $V_t(s)\ge V^*(s)-\eta$; and $V_t(s)-V^{\pi_t}_{M_{K_t}}(s)\le\eta$ for every state. On this event, the total number of value-table rebuilds plus selections of pairs outside $K_t$ is at most $(m+1)|E_\eta|$.

thm-pac-mdp-escape-event-reduction.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let a learning algorithm interact with a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP. Suppose constants $B,W,Q_c$ satisfy $0<B$, $0<W\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<Q_c\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and $V^*(s)\le B$. The learner maintains $0\le Q_t(s,a)\le Q_c$ and, whenever $(s,a)\notin K_t$, $Q_t(s,a)\le W$. Put $V_t(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q_t(s,a)$, and let $\pi_t$ be the deterministic greedy policy under a fixed tie order. Before acting at time $t$, let $K_t$ be a history-measurable set of known pairs; assume it stays fixed until a Q-value update or a selection of a pair outside $K_t$. Write $M_t=M_{K_t}(Q_t)$ for the known-state/action MDP and $C=B+W$. For parameters $0<\eta\le C$ with $\eta(1-\gamma)<1$ and $0<\rho<1/2$, suppose that with probability at least $1-\rho$, simultaneously for every $t,s$,
$$V_t(s)\ge V^*(s)-\eta,\qquad V_t(s)-V^{\pi_t}_{M_t}(s)\le\eta,$$
and the total number of Q-update times plus outside-$K_t$ selection times is at most an integer $\zeta\ge0$. Define $q=\eta/(2C)$, set
$$H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil \ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(1/\rho)}{q}\right\rceil.$$
Then, with probability at least $1-2\rho$, the PAC-MDP count satisfies $N_{4\eta}\le HM$. Here $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.

lem-delayed-q-learning-optimism-and-upda.interface:
## Statement

Fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an admissible heuristic with cap $V_{\max}$, and $0<\epsilon_1<1$. Put $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $\kappa=\lceil SA V_{\max}/\epsilon_1\rceil$, $N=SA(1+\kappa)$, and $C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max}$. Run Delayed Q-learning with a positive integer $m$ satisfying
$$m\ge\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{8N}{\delta}\right\rceil\qquad(0<\delta<1).$$
For $V_t(s)=\max_aQ_t(s,a)$, define
$$K_t=\left\{(s,a):Q_t(s,a)-\left(r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V_t(s')\right)\le3\epsilon_1\right\}.$$
With probability at least $1-\delta$, all estimates remain optimistic, $Q_t(s,a)\ge Q^*(s,a)$ for every $t,s,a$; every attempted update whose first sample is taken with its pair outside $K_t$ succeeds; the number of successful updates is at most
$$G=\sum_{s,a}\left(1+\frac{D(s,a)}{\epsilon_1}\right);$$
and the number of visits selecting a pair outside $K_t$ is at most $2mG$. The additive $1$ in each pair's update allowance is necessary, including when $U(s,a)=V^*(s)$.

thm-r-max-pac-bound.interface:
## Statement

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0<\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad b=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{64V_{\max}},\quad m=\left\lceil\frac{8(S+\ln(16SA/\delta))}{b^2}\right\rceil,\quad \beta=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}{16},$$
and run R-MAX with sample threshold $m$ and value-iteration tolerance $\beta$. Let $E_\eta=\{(s,a):U(s,a)\ge V^*(s)-\eta\}$ and $\zeta=(m+1)|E_\eta|$. Define $q=\eta/(4V_{\max})$, and define $H$ and $M$ by
$$H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. For the uninformative heuristic $U(s,a)=V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, the bound is $\widetilde O(S^2A/[\epsilon^3(1-\gamma)^6])$, where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors.

thm-delayed-q-learning-pac-bound.interface:
## Statement

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, write $S=|S|$ and $A=\max_s|A(s)|$, and fix $0<\epsilon<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, $0<\delta<1$, and an admissible heuristic with normalized cap $V_{\max}$. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Otherwise put
$$\eta=\epsilon/4,\quad \epsilon_1=\frac{\eta(1-\gamma)}3,\quad \kappa=\left\lceil\frac{SA V_{\max}}{\epsilon_1}\right\rceil,\quad N=SA(1+\kappa),\quad C_1=1+\gamma V_{\max},$$
and choose
$$m=\left\lceil\frac{C_1^2}{2\epsilon_1^2}\ln\frac{16N}{\delta}\right\rceil.$$
Run Delayed Q-learning with $m$ and $\epsilon_1$. Write $D(s,a)=[U(s,a)-V^*(s)]_+$, $G=\sum_{s,a}(1+D(s,a)/\epsilon_1)$, and $\zeta=\lceil(2m+1)G\rceil$. Define $q,H,M$ by
$$q=\frac{\eta}{4V_{\max}},\qquad H=\begin{cases}1,&\gamma=0,\\ \max\{1,\lceil\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)])/(-\ln\gamma)\rceil\},&0<\gamma<1,\end{cases}\qquad M=\left\lceil\frac{2(\zeta+1)+2\ln(2/\delta)}q\right\rceil.$$
Then $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$. Equivalently, up to logarithmic factors, the bound is
$$\widetilde O\!\left(\frac{V_{\max}(1+\gamma V_{\max})^2\left[\sum_{s,a}D(s,a)+SA\epsilon(1-\gamma)\right]}{\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^4}\right),$$
where $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The additive term remains when all heuristic slacks vanish. For $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ this gives $\widetilde O(SA/[\epsilon^4(1-\gamma)^8])$.

def-policy-bellman-operator.interface:
## Definition

For a finite MDP, a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the **policy Bellman operator** $T^\pi:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^\pi V)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set.interface:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
([[def-equinumerous]]), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of [[def-finite-sum]] when the
values are real and of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
[[lem-finite-sum-permutation-invariance]] to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of [[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]]
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]).

## Remarks

- **This is a different object from $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, and the bridge is what
  keeps them one notion.** The sum over an initial segment is indexed by a
  natural number and needs no well-definedness argument; the sum over a finite
  set is indexed by an arbitrary finite set and is well posed only because a
  finite sum is permutation invariant. Clause (a) is the statement that the
  second restricts to the first.

- **Splitting the index set** — the identity
  $\sum_{i \in S \cup T} a_i = \sum_{i \in S} a_i + \sum_{i \in T} a_i$ for
  disjoint finite $S$ and $T$, and its version for a finite partition — is not
  proved here but in [[thm-sum-rule]], the next item, whose splice bijection is
  exactly what such a proof needs. Keeping the two together avoids building the
  same bijection twice.

- **Three notions of finite sum will exist in the library**: over an initial
  segment ([[def-finite-sum]]), over a finite index set (here), and in an
  arbitrary monoid ([[def-monoid-finite-product]], later in the reading order).
  Each is introduced with its bridge to the previous one, which is what stops
  them drifting apart.

lem-finite-span-orthogonal-projection-in.interface:
## Statement

Let $H$ be a real inner-product space and $V\subseteq H$ a finite-dimensional
subspace. For each $f\in H$ there is a unique $p\in V$ such that $f-p$ is
orthogonal to $V$, meaning $\langle f-p,v\rangle=0$ for every $v\in V$.
For every $v\in V$,
$$\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2.$$
In particular, $\|f\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|f-p\|^2$.

lem-projected-bellman-error-is-well-defi.interface:
## Statement

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set of a finite Markov decision process, let $0\leq\gamma<1$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Define the policy Bellman operator by
$$
(T^\pi f)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)f(s')\right].
$$
Let $\mu:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)=1$, and let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_d:S\to\mathbb R$ be a finite list of feature functions. Define $f\sim_\mu g$ when $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)(f(s)-g(s))^2=0$, let $H_\mu$ be the quotient of $\mathbb R^S$ by this relation, and define $\langle[f]_\mu,[g]_\mu\rangle_\mu=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)f(s)g(s)$. Then this quotient is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. The span $V_\mu$ of $[\phi_1]_\mu,\ldots,[\phi_d]_\mu$ is finite-dimensional, and every $h\in H_\mu$ has a unique orthogonal projection $\Pi_\mu h\in V_\mu$. Here orthogonal means that $h-\Pi_\mu h$ has inner product zero with every vector in $V_\mu$. For each fixed $w\in\mathbb R^d$, put $v_w(s)=\sum_{j=1}^d\phi_j(s)w_j$ and $\delta_w=[T^\pi v_w-v_w]_\mu$. Then $\|\delta_w\|_\mu^2$ and $\|\Pi_\mu\delta_w\|_\mu^2$ are well-defined real numbers, including when some state weights vanish or the features are linearly dependent.

def-projected-bellman-error.interface:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set of a finite Markov decision process, let $0\leq\gamma<1$, let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy, and let $\mu:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)=1$. The function $\mu$ is a fixed state-weighting distribution; it need not be stationary for $\pi$. Let $d$ be a positive integer, let $\phi:S\to\mathbb R^d$ be a feature map, and for $w\in\mathbb R^d$ put $v_w(s)=\phi(s)^\mathsf T w$.

For real functions $f,g:S\to\mathbb R$, write $f\sim_\mu g$ when $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)(f(s)-g(s))^2=0$. Let $[f]_\mu$ denote the equivalence class of $f$ and define $\langle[f]_{\mu},[g]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)f(s)g(s)$ and $\|[f]_\mu\|_\mu^2=\langle[f]_{\mu},[f]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu$. Let $H_\mu$ be the resulting finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let $V_\mu$ be the span in $H_\mu$ of the equivalence classes of the $d$ coordinate feature functions.

For $h\in H_\mu$, let $\Pi_\mu h$ be the unique vector in $V_\mu$ whose difference from $h$ is orthogonal to every vector in $V_\mu$. The Bellman-error vector for $v_w$ is $\delta_w=[T^\pi v_w-v_w]_\mu$. Define the mean square Bellman error and mean square projected Bellman error by $\operatorname{BE}_\mu(w)=\|\delta_w\|_\mu^2$ and $\operatorname{PBE}_\mu(w)=\|\Pi_\mu\delta_w\|_\mu^2$.

def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-an.interface:
## Definition

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

thm-finite-mdp-policy-induces-reward-sta.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Put $E=S\times(\mathcal R\cup\{0\})$ with its discrete sigma-algebra and define, for $x=(s,\eta)\in E$ and $B\subseteq E$,

$$ K_\pi(x,B)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s) \sum_{\substack{s'\in S\\\rho\in\mathcal R}}1_B(s',\rho)\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$
