Then $K_\pi$ is a probability kernel on $E$. For each initial state $s\in S$, there is a probability law on $E^{\mathbb N}$ whose coordinate process starts at $(s,0)$ and is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K_\pi$ relative to its natural filtration.

thm-bairds-counterexample-off-policy-td-.interface:
## Statement

Let the states be $S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_7\}$ and the two actions available at each state be $\mathrm{dashed}$ and $\mathrm{solid}$. All rewards are zero and $\gamma=0.99$. Under $\mathrm{dashed}$, the next state is each of $s_1,\ldots,s_6$ with probability $1/6$; under $\mathrm{solid}$, the next state is $s_7$ with probability $1$. The behavior policy has $b(\mathrm{dashed}\mid s)=6/7$ and $b(\mathrm{solid}\mid s)=1/7$ at every state, and the target policy selects $\mathrm{solid}$ with probability $1$. Use the uniform state weighting $\mu(s)=1/7$. For standard basis vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_8$ of $\mathbb R^8$, set $\phi(s_i)=2e_i+e_8$ for $1\leq i\leq6$ and $\phi(s_7)=e_7+2e_8$, and define $v_w(s)=\phi(s)^\mathsf T w$. For a behavior transition $(S,A,S')$, draw $S$ from $\mu$, draw $A$ from $b(\cdot\mid S)$, and draw $S'$ from the stated action transition law. Put $\rho=\pi(A\mid S)/b(A\mid S)$ and $\delta=\gamma v_w(S')-v_w(S)$, and define the expected semi-gradient TD(0) update by $\bar w^+=w+\alpha\,\mathbb E_{\mu,b}[\rho\delta\,\phi(S)]$. Also define the synchronous expected dynamic-programming update by $w^+=w+\frac{\alpha}{7}\sum_{s\in S}\big((T^\pi v_w)(s)-v_w(s)\big)\phi(s)$. For every step size $\alpha>0$, both deterministic update sequences starting at $w_0=(1,1,1,1,1,1,10,1)$ have Euclidean norm $\|w\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^8w_i^2)^{1/2}$ tending to infinity. This is a claim about the stated expected/deterministic updates; it asserts no probability-one divergence result for individual stochastic TD trajectories.

thm-bellman-error-unlearnability-example.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice to form the infinite trajectory laws. Fix $0\leq\gamma<1$. An actionless finite Markov reward process (MRP) here means a nonempty finite state set with a joint probability law for next state and reward at each state. Consider the following two MRPs, each with its stated stationary state-weighting distribution, meaning that one transition leaves the distribution unchanged.

In MRP 1 the state set is $\{A,B\}$, with transitions $A\to B$ receiving reward $0$ deterministically and $B\to A$ receiving reward $1$ with probability $1/2$ or $B\to B$ receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\mu_1(A)=1/3$, $\mu_1(B)=2/3$.

In MRP 2 the state set is $\{A,B,B'\}$, with transitions $A\to B$ and $A\to B'$ each receiving reward $0$ with probability $1/2$, $B\to A$ receiving reward $1$ deterministically, and $B'\to B$ or $B'\to B'$ each receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\mu_2(A)=\mu_2(B)=\mu_2(B')=1/3$.

In both processes the observed feature is $\psi(A)=(1,0)$ and $\psi(B)=\psi(B')=(0,1)$, so a parameter $w=(a,b)^\mathsf T$ assigns values $v_w(A)=a$ and $v_w(B)=v_w(B')=b$. Starting from the stated stationary weighting, the two processes induce the same probability law on the observed feature/reward sequence $((\psi(S_n),R_{n+1}))_{n\geq0}$. Their mean square Bellman errors, defined as the stationary-weighted square of the conditional expected one-step TD error, are
$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{BE}_1(a,b)&=\frac13(\gamma b-a)^2+\frac23\left(\frac{\gamma}{2}(a+b)-b\right)^2,\\ \operatorname{BE}_2(a,b)&=\frac13\left((\gamma b-a)^2+(1+\gamma a-b)^2+(-1+(\gamma-1)b)^2\right).\end{aligned}
$$
MRP 1 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=(0,0)$ and minimum $0$. With $D=1+\gamma+\gamma^2$, MRP 2 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=\left(-\frac{\gamma}{D},\frac{\gamma}{2D}\right)$ and minimum $\frac{(\gamma+2)^2}{6D}$; also $\operatorname{BE}_2(0,0)=2/3$. For every $0<\gamma<1$ the minimizing parameters differ. Thus the Bellman-error objective and, for positive discount, its minimizing parameter are not determined by the observable feature/reward sequence law. An MRP here has no action-dependent policy; it is not an unseen-action offline-MDP policy-impossibility claim.

def-total-variation-distance-for-probabi.interface:
## Definition

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a.interface:
## Statement

Let $E$ be an at most countable set equipped with the power-set
$\sigma$-algebra $2^E$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be probability laws on $E$
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]). Then

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{x\in E}\bigl|\mu(x)-\nu(x)\bigr| ,$$

where $\mu(x),\nu(x)$ denote the singleton masses and the series on the right
is a series of nonnegative numbers in $[0,+\infty]$. The value is finite; it is
$0$ exactly when $\mu=\nu$. The supremum defining the total variation distance
is attained at the event $A_+=\{x\in E:\mu(x)>\nu(x)\}$.

lem-of-triangle-inequality.interface:
## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

def-learned-mdp-model.interface:
## Definition

Let the true environment be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, a finite reward alphabet contained in $[0,1]$, and joint next-state/reward probabilities $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$, and let $r(s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ be the expected reward and next-state probabilities obtained by summing this joint law. A finite learned model on the same state and action sets consists of estimates $\hat r:D\to[0,1]$ and probability distributions $\hat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every $(s,a)\in D$. The estimated transition table is a probability kernel on the finite discrete spaces.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, define the reward error $e_r(s,a)=|r(s,a)-\hat r(s,a)|$ and transition error

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. These are uniform expected-reward and total-variation errors on $C$; the learned model definition makes no accuracy assertion.

def-finite-stochastic-shortest-path-prob.interface:
## Definition

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each $g\in G$ has a single dummy action that returns to $g$ with reward $0$ with probability $1$. For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

lem-total-variation-coupling-and-kernel-.interface:
## Statement

Let $\mu,\nu$ be probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and let
$P$ be a probability kernel on that space. Then
$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{f:\mathsf X\to[0,1]\ \mathcal X\text{-measurable}}\left|\int f\,d\mu-\int f\,d\nu\right|,$$
$$\lVert\mu P-\nu P\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}.$$
If $(U,V)$ is a coupling of $\mu$ and $\nu$ on a probability space and
$E$ is a measurable event on which $U=V$, then
$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\rm TV}\le\mathbb P(E^c).$$

thm-monotone-convergence.interface:
## Statement

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $S$ is bounded
   above ([[def-bounded-set]]), then $(x_k)$ converges ([[def-real-limit]]) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) supplies the
first and [[thm-infimum-property]] the second, and each is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

def-finite-horizon-mdp-return.interface:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite action set for each $s\in S$, let $r(s,a)\in[0,1]$, and let $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ be a probability distribution on $S$ for each admissible pair. A finite-horizon Markov policy of horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ with $H\ge1$ is a family of probability distributions $\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)$ on $A(s)$ for $0\le t<H$. Given an initial state distribution $\mu$, define $d_0=\mu$ and, for $0\le t<H-1$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a).$$

The finite-horizon expected return is

$$J_H(M,\mu,\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a).$$

The same definition applies to a learned model by replacing $r,P$ with its estimated reward and transition tables. It is the expected sum of the $H$ one-step rewards; no discount factor or terminal continuation value is included.

lem-finite-policy-kernel-tv-propagation.interface:
## Statement

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, let $A(s)$ be finite and nonempty for each $s\in S$, and let $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ and $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ be probability distributions on $S$ for each admissible pair. For distributions $u,v$ on $S$, write $\operatorname{TV}(u,v)=\frac12\sum_{x\in S}|u(x)-v(x)|$. Let $\pi(\cdot\mid s)$ be a probability distribution on $A(s)$ for each state. Define the induced transition rows

$$K^\pi(s,x)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(x\mid s,a),\qquad \widehat K^\pi(s,x)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat P(x\mid s,a).$$

If $d$ and $\widehat d$ are probability distributions on $S$ and, for some $\epsilon\ge0$,

$$\operatorname{TV}(P(\cdot\mid s,a),\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a))\le\epsilon$$

whenever $\widehat d(s)>0$ and $\pi(a\mid s)>0$, then

$$\operatorname{TV}(dK^\pi,\widehat d\widehat K^\pi)\le\operatorname{TV}(d,\widehat d)+\epsilon.$$

Here $dK^\pi$ and $\widehat d\widehat K^\pi$ are the next-state distributions obtained by applying the indicated transition rows.

thm-finite-stochastic-shortest-path-valu.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let a finite positive-cost stochastic shortest-path problem have at least one proper stationary policy. For any policy $\sigma$ whose action distribution may depend on the entire finite history, use its trajectory law from the initial state $s$ and define

$$J^\sigma(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E_s^\sigma\!\left[c(S_t,A_t)\,1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}\right],$$

where $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)>0$ off the absorbing goal set $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. The optimal total cost $f^*(s)=\inf_\sigma J^\sigma(s)$ is finite for every state. It is the unique finite nonnegative function satisfying

$$f^*(g)=0\quad(g\in G),\qquad f^*(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}\left[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)f^*(s')\right]\quad(s\notin G).$$

The minimum is attained by a deterministic stationary policy that is proper and has total cost $f^*$ from every initial state.

alg-real-time-dynamic-programming.interface:
## Definition

Input: a finite stochastic shortest-path model, a finite value table $V_0:S\to\mathbb R$ with $V_0(g)=0$ on goals, a nonempty finite start set $S_0\subseteq S\setminus G$, a positive integer trial cap $L$, and an infinite supplied start sequence in which each member of $S_0$ occurs infinitely often. For each trial, set the current state to the next supplied start. For at most $L$ decision steps, or until a goal is reached, do the following: at the current nonglobal state $s$, compute

$$q_V(s,a)=r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\qquad(a\in A(s)),$$

choose uniformly from the nonempty set of actions attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using a fresh tie draw, execute the chosen action in the given MDP and observe the next state, then replace $V(s)$ by $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using the value table from before that backup. Keep every other value unchanged. At a goal keep value $0$. After a trial ends, reset the state to the next supplied start without resetting the value table. The procedure returns the successive value tables and selected actions; it asserts no convergence guarantee by itself.

alg-model-predictive-control.interface:
## Definition

Input: a finite learned MDP model, a current state $s_0$, a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ with $H\ge1$, and a finite action listing at each state for deterministic tie-breaking. Initialize $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. For $h=1,\ldots,H$, compute for every admissible pair

$$Q_h(s,a)=\hat r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}\hat P(s'\mid s,a)V_{h-1}(s'),\qquad V_h(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q_h(s,a).$$

At the current state $s_0$, return the first action in its supplied listing that attains $V_H(s_0)$. The controller executes only this first action in the true environment, observes the next state, and may invoke the procedure again with the new state and a newly supplied learned model. The procedure specifies no model-update rule and makes no guarantee about the true return of the model-selected action.

thm-single-policy-finite-horizon-simulat.interface:
## Statement

Let $M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},r,P)$ and $\widehat M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},\widehat r,\widehat P)$ be finite models on a common nonempty finite state set and common nonempty finite action sets, with $r,\widehat r\in[0,1]$ and probability transition rows. Fix a horizon $H\ge1$, a common initial state law $\mu$, and one possibly time-dependent randomized Markov policy $\pi=(\pi_t)_{t=0}^{H-1}$. Let $d_t$ and $\widehat d_t$ be the state occupancies under $M$ and $\widehat M$, respectively, starting from $d_0=\widehat d_0=\mu$. Define

$$C_H^\pi=\{(s,a): d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\text{ or }\widehat d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\text{ for some }0\le t<H\}.$$

Suppose $|r(s,a)-\widehat r(s,a)|\le\epsilon_r$ and $\operatorname{TV}(P(\cdot\mid s,a),\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a))\le\epsilon_p$ for every $(s,a)\in C_H^\pi$, where $\operatorname{TV}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{s'}|p(s')-q(s')|$. Then

$$|J_H(M,\mu,\pi)-J_H(\widehat M,\mu,\pi)|\le H\epsilon_r+\binom{H}{2}\epsilon_p.$$

The guarantee concerns this fixed policy and the stated reachable pairs; it does not bound the policy selected by optimizing the learned model.

def-model-exploitation.interface:
## Definition

Let $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ be a finite state-action domain, let $B\subseteq D$ be the pairs observed at least once in a data set, fix a horizon $H\ge1$ and initial state law $\mu$, and let $\Pi$ be any finite nonempty class of deterministic time-dependent Markov policies for that horizon. For a policy $\pi\in\Pi$, compute its expected return under the true model and learned model using $d_0=\mu$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a),\qquad J_H(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a),$$

and analogously $\widehat J_H(\pi)$ using $\widehat P,\widehat r$. The learned-model occupancy of a pair $(s,a)$ at time $t$ is $\widehat d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)$. A model-optimal policy is any $\widehat\pi\in\Pi$ attaining $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat J_H(\pi)$. Such a policy **exploits the model off support relative to $B$** if it has positive learned-model occupancy on at least one pair in $D\setminus B$, overestimates its own true return $\widehat J_H(\widehat\pi)>J_H(\widehat\pi)$, and is truly suboptimal within $\Pi$: $J_H(\widehat\pi)<\max_{\pi\in\Pi}J_H(\pi)$. This definition describes a failure mode; it is not a performance claim about every model optimizer.

def-integrable-real-and-complex-function.interface:
## Definition

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

lem-finite-mdp-policy-action-state-rewar.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$ and let

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

with its discrete sigma-algebra. There is a probability law on $S\times Z^{\mathbb N}$ whose first state is $S_0=s_0$ and whose subsequent coordinates are $Z_n=(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. For every $m\ge0$ and every feasible finite trajectory $(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)$, its probability is

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\pi(a_n\mid s_n)\,p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a_n),
$$

where the empty product for $m=0$ is $1$.

Its state-reward marginal also has the finite-prefix probabilities

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a\in A(s_n)}\pi(a\mid s_n)p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a)
$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

def-offline-reinforcement-learning-datas.interface:
## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy-induced path laws below. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, and let $\mathcal R\subset\mathbb R$ be a finite nonempty reward set. A finite Markov decision process here consists of these sets and a joint next-state/reward probability mass $p(s',r\mid s,a)\ge0$, defined for $s,s'\in S$, $a\in A(s)$, and $r\in\mathcal R$, with $\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}p(s',r\mid s,a)=1$ for every $(s,a)$. A stationary Markov policy $\sigma$ assigns probabilities $\sigma(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sigma(a\mid s)=1$ at every state.

Fix a horizon $H\ge1$, a discount $0\le\gamma\le1$, and an initial state $s_0\in S$. A trajectory is a tuple $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{H-1},r_H,s_H)$ with $s_t\in S$, $a_t\in A(s_t)$, and $r_{t+1}\in\mathcal R$ for each $0\le t<H$. Write $\Omega_H$ for the finite set of all such tuples. For each stationary policy $\sigma$, let $P^\sigma_H$ be the probability law on $\Omega_H$ whose atom masses are

$$P^\sigma_H(\{\tau\})=\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\sigma(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t).$$

For a trajectory $\tau$, its finite-horizon return is $G_H(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}$, and the value of target policy $\pi$ from $s_0$ is $J_H(\pi;s_0)=\int_{\Omega_H}G_H\,dP^\pi_H$. A fixed logged dataset of size $n\ge1$ consists of independent trajectories $(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n)$, each with law $P^\mu_H$ for a behavior policy $\mu$; the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$ used to generate the data are known. Full horizon coverage means $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$, so every behavior-null trajectory event is also target-null. In this finite setting, the condition $\pi(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow\mu(a\mid s)>0$ at every state-action pair reachable under $\pi$ before time $H$ is sufficient for full horizon coverage. A trajectory function is integrable under a law $P$ when $\int_{\Omega_H}|f|\,dP<\infty$. All returns are integrable in this finite-horizon finite-reward setting; importance-weighted return expressions below are used only when they are integrable.

def-radon-nikodym-derivative.interface:
## Definition

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure.

1. If $\nu$ is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable real-valued functions $f$ satisfying the measurable-set integral formula in that theorem.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), if $\nu$ is a finite complex measure and $\nu\ll\mu$, the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** $d\nu/d\mu$ is the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equivalence class of complex $L^1(\mu)$ functions $h$ satisfying
   $$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A),$$
   as given by [[cor-finite-complex-measures-admit-integrable-radon-nikodym-densities]].

In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]].

thm-chain-rule-for-radon-nikodym-derivat.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite positive measures and let $\nu$ be a
signed measure or a finite complex measure on the same measurable space.
Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$
with $\bigcup_nX_n=X$, $\lambda(X_n)<+\infty$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and
$|\nu|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$, and assume $\nu\ll\mu\ll\lambda$. Then
$$\frac{d\nu}{d\lambda}=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}\qquad\lambda\text{-almost everywhere.}$$

thm-integration-against-a-density.interface:
## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-.interface:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

lem-finite-horizon-trajectory-ratio-is-r.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC and the finite-horizon dataset conditions of the preceding definition, with full horizon coverage $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$. For $0\le t<H$, let $\Omega_{t+1}$ be the finite set of trajectory prefixes through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, and let $P^\sigma_{t+1}$ be the marginal law of this prefix under policy $\sigma\in\{\pi,\mu\}$. On a behavior-positive prefix define

$$W_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)},$$

and set $W_{0:t}=0$ on behavior-null prefixes. Then $P^\pi_{t+1}\ll P^\mu_{t+1}$, and $W_{0:t}$ is a version of $dP^\pi_{t+1}/dP^\mu_{t+1}$ up to $P^\mu_{t+1}$-almost-everywhere equality. In particular, for every real $G$ integrable under $P^\pi_H$, the full-horizon weight $W_{0:H-1}$ satisfies

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}G]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[G],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}|G|]<\infty.$$

The same identity holds prefixwise: for each $0\le t<H$ and every real $g$ integrable under $P^\pi_{t+1}$, with $g$ evaluated on the observed prefix,

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}g]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[g],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}|g|]<\infty.$$

alg-trajectory-importance-sampling-ope.interface:
## Definition

Assume AC for the policy-induced trajectory laws. Input a finite-horizon logged dataset of $n\ge1$ independent behavior trajectories, a target policy $\pi$, the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$, horizon $H$, and discount $0\le\gamma\le1$. Require full horizon coverage $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$. For trajectory $i$, compute $\rho_{i,t}=\pi(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)/\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)$ for $0\le t<H$, and $W_{i,t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\rho_{i,k}$; set $W_{i,-1}=1$. If an observed pair has $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0<\pi(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)$, return status unsupported; if both probabilities are zero, set that ratio to zero. Let $G_i=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_{t+1}^i$. Return the ordinary trajectory estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{OIS}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n W_{i,H-1}G_i,$$

the per-decision estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{PDIS}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tW_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i,$$

and the self-normalized weighted estimator

$$\widehat J_{\mathrm{WIS}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}G_i}{\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}},&\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}>0,\\0,&\sum_{i=1}^nW_{i,H-1}=0.\end{cases}$$

All three outputs are finite under the finite-MDP, finite-horizon and coverage hypotheses. The procedure specifies estimators; it includes no finite-sample unbiasedness assertion for the self-normalized output.

alg-doubly-robust-ope.interface:
## Definition

Assume AC for the behavior-policy trajectory law. Input a finite-horizon logged dataset with $n\ge1$ behavior trajectories, a target policy $\pi$, finite real functions $\widehat Q_t(s,a)$ for $0\le t<H$, and finite nonnegative action-weight multipliers $\widehat\rho_t(s,a)$ for $0\le t<H$. Hold the functions and multipliers fixed when taking expectation over the evaluation dataset; they may be conditioned on an independent training sample. Define $\widehat V_H(s)=0$ for every $s$, and for $t=H-1,\ldots,0$ define

$$\widehat V_t(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat Q_t(s,a).$$

For each logged trajectory $i$, set $\widehat W_{i,-1}=1$ and $\widehat W_{i,t}=\widehat W_{i,t-1}\widehat\rho_t(S_t^i,A_t^i)$ for $0\le t<H$. Compute

$$D_i=\widehat V_0(s_0)+\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\widehat W_{i,t}\left(R_{t+1}^i+\gamma\widehat V_{t+1}(S_{t+1}^i)-\widehat Q_t(S_t^i,A_t^i)\right),$$

and return $\widehat J_{\mathrm{DR}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD_i$. When supplied as propensity ratios, the multipliers have the form $\widehat\rho_t(s,a)=\pi(a\mid s)/\widetilde\mu_t(a\mid s)$, with positive denominators on target-positive actions. In the exact-ratio case they equal the target-to-behavior action-likelihood factors $\pi(a\mid s)/\mu(a\mid s)$; the procedure also permits finite fitted multipliers for the correct-value-model case. The fixed terminal value $\widehat V_H=0$ is part of the procedure.

thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-ra.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.

thm-offline-coverage-impossibility-examp.interface:
## Statement

There are two finite one-step Markov decision processes with the same logged-data law under one behavior policy, but different target-policy values and different uniquely optimal actions. A finite one-step Markov decision process here has a finite state set, finite nonempty action sets, a finite reward set, and a probability mass on the next-state/reward pair for every state/action pair. Let the state set be $\{s_0,z\}$, the action sets be $A(s_0)=\{a,b\}$ and $A(z)=\{c\}$, the reward set be $\{-1,0,1\}$, and the horizon be $H=1$. In both processes, action $a$ at $s_0$ gives reward $0$ and moves to $z$, and action $c$ at $z$ gives reward $0$ and stays at $z$. In process $M_+$, action $b$ at $s_0$ gives reward $1$ and moves to $z$; in process $M_-$, it gives reward $-1$ and moves to $z$. The behavior policy chooses $a$ at $s_0$ with probability $1$, while the target policy chooses $b$ there with probability $1$; both policies choose $c$ at $z$ with probability $1$. Every behavior-generated logged trajectory is $(s_0,a,0,z)$ in both processes, so every sample size $n\ge1$ has the same logged-data law in $M_+$ and $M_-$. The target value is the expected one-step reward: it is $1$ in $M_+$ and $-1$ in $M_-$, and the unique value-maximizing initial action is $b$ in $M_+$ and $a$ in $M_-$. An estimator here is a real-valued function of the logged dataset; it is unbiased for a target value when its expectation under the logged-data law equals that value. Consequently, no such estimator can be unbiased for the target value in both processes, and no data-based action selector can identify the unique optimal initial action with certainty in both.

thm-doubly-robust-ope-is-unbiased-under-.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC and the finite-horizon dataset conditions with fixed target policy $\pi$, behavior policy $\mu$, horizon $H$, discount $0\le\gamma\le1$, and initial state $s_0$. Hold the finite functions $\widehat Q_t$ and multipliers $\widehat\rho_t$ fixed when taking expectation over the evaluation trajectories. Set $\widehat V_H(s)=0$ and $\widehat V_t(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat Q_t(s,a)$. Let

$$D(\tau)=\widehat V_0(s_0)+\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\widehat W_{0:t}(\tau)\left(R_{t+1}+\gamma\widehat V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})-\widehat Q_t(S_t,A_t)\right),\qquad \widehat W_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\widehat\rho_k(S_k,A_k).$$

For a dataset of $n$ independent evaluation trajectories, let $\widehat J_{\mathrm{DR}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD(\tau_i)$. Then $\mathbb E[\widehat J_{\mathrm{DR}}]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$ under either of these separate conditions:

1. The full target trajectory law is absolutely continuous with respect to the behavior trajectory law, and every multiplier is the correct action ratio $\widehat\rho_t(s,a)=\pi(a\mid s)/\mu(a\mid s)$ on every behavior-positive state-action pair reachable before time $H$; the ratio is $0$ when $\pi(a\mid s)=0<\mu(a\mid s)$. No correctness assumption is imposed on the functions $\widehat Q_t$.

2. For every $0\le t<H$, state $s$, and action $a$, the value model is exact:

   $$\widehat Q_t(s,a)=Q_t^\pi(s,a):=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}p(s',r\mid s,a)\left(r+\gamma V_{t+1}^\pi(s')\right),\qquad V_H^\pi(s)=0,\qquad V_t^\pi(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)Q_t^\pi(s,a),$$

   so $\widehat V_t=V_t^\pi$ at every step, including the zero terminal value. This branch requires no trajectory coverage and no correctness assumption on the fixed finite multipliers. If neither exact condition holds, this theorem asserts no unbiasedness.

lem-a-double-sum-over-finite-index-sets-.interface:
## Statement

Let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets and let $a : S \times T \to \mathbb{R}$, or
$a : S \times T \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_{ij}$ for $a(i,j)$. Then $S \times T$
is finite and

$$\sum_{i \in S}\Big(\sum_{j \in T} a_{ij}\Big) \;=\; \sum_{p \in S \times T} a_p \;=\; \sum_{j \in T}\Big(\sum_{i \in S} a_{ij}\Big),$$

all three sums being the sums over a finite index set of
[[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]], carried by [[def-finite-sum]] when the
values are real and by [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] when they are natural.

**This is not a clause of [[thm-sum-rule]].** That theorem splits one sum along a
partition of *its own* index set; the identity above exchanges the roles of two
*different* index sets, and it is what an argument that counts a set of pairs in
two ways needs. Both outer index sets may be empty, in which case all three
quantities are $0$ (respectively $1$ for the product form of the underlying
recursion), since a sum over the empty index set is the empty sum.

lem-finite-horizon-mdp-policy-occupancy.interface:
## Statement

Let a finite Markov decision process have a nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$, with state transition probabilities $P(s'\mid s,a)$ obtained by summing its joint reward-transition law over rewards. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer, let $\mu_0:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu_0(s)=1$, and let $\pi(a\mid s)$ be a stationary Markov policy. Define recursively

$$\mu_{t+1}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\mu_t(s)\pi(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a),\qquad 0\le t<T.$$

Then each $\mu_t$ is a probability vector on $S$, and the finite-horizon average occupancy

$$d_\pi(s)=\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mu_t(s)$$

is also a probability vector. This construction uses only finite sums and does not require an infinite-path probability extension.

def-imitation-learning-and-expert-surrog.interface:
## Definition

Fix a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state, a positive integer horizon $T$, and an initial probability vector $\mu_0$ on $S$. A **policy** is a stationary Markov policy $\pi(a\mid s)$; a **deterministic expert** is a function $\pi^*:S\to\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$ with $\pi^*(s)\in A(s)$. For a policy $\pi$, let $\mu_t^\pi$ and $d_\pi$ be the finite-horizon state and average-occupancy probability vectors defined by the finite recursion in the preceding lemma.

Let $c_t(s,a)\in[0,1]$ be the task cost at time $t$ for $0\le t<T$. Define the total expected task cost by

$$J(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)c_t(s,a).$$

Define the expert cost-to-go recursively by $V_T^*(s)=0$ and, for $0\le t<T$,

$$Q_t^*(s,a)=c_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}^*(s'),\qquad V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s)).$$

For a learner policy $\pi_\theta$ indexed by a parameter $\theta$ in a nonempty set $K$, define its expert-action disagreement probability at $s$ by $e(s,\theta)=\sum_{a\in A(s):a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$. An **expert surrogate loss** is a function $\ell:S\times K\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\ell(s,\theta)\ge e(s,\theta)$ for every $s\in S$ and $\theta\in K$. The average surrogate loss under a policy's own state occupancy is $\mathbb E_{s\sim d_{\pi_\theta}}[\ell(s,\theta)]=\sum_s d_{\pi_\theta}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$.

**Behavior cloning** fits a learner policy using expert labels on states sampled from $d_{\pi^*}$. **DAgger** (Dataset Aggregation) is the interactive alternative: at iteration $i$, it rolls out a mixture $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$, where $\hat\pi_i$ is the current learner and $\beta_i\in[0,1]$ is the expert-use probability at each decision, queries the expert on the visited states, aggregates those labeled states with prior data, and updates the learner. In the infinite-sample analysis define $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$. When the minimum is attained, define $\epsilon_N=\min_{\theta\in K}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta)$ and the learner's average regret $\gamma_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\epsilon_N$. Labels under learner-induced states require interaction with the expert; fixed demonstrations alone do not supply them.

alg-dagger.interface:
## Definition

Let a finite-horizon imitation-learning problem have the finite MDP, initial state distribution, positive integer horizon $T$, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner class $\{\pi_\theta:\theta\in K\}$, and expert surrogate loss $\ell(s,\theta)$ defined previously. Let $N\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be integers giving the number of training rounds and trajectories per round, let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N\in[0,1]$ be expert-use probabilities, supply an initial parameter $\theta_1\in K$, and supply a deterministic selector for attained minimizers of the cumulative losses. Require that each cumulative training-loss function below attains a minimum on $K$; when the minimizer is unique the selector returns it.

For each round $i=1,\ldots,N$:

1. Set $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$. At each of the $T$ decision times, independently choose the expert action with probability $\beta_i$ and otherwise choose the action of $\hat\pi_i$. This per-decision stochastic policy is $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$.
2. Run $m$ trajectories of length $T$ from the specified initial distribution using $\pi_i$. At every visited state $S_{ij t}$, for $1\le j\le m$ and $0\le t<T$, query and record the expert label $\pi^*(S_{ij t})$. The expert label is recorded for training and is not executed unless the mixture in step 1 selected the expert.
3. Define the empirical round loss on every candidate parameter by

   $$\hat L_i(\theta)=\frac1{mT}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ij t},\theta).$$

4. Aggregate all labeled state/action pairs from this round with the previous dataset. Update by Follow-the-Leader on the cumulative aggregate loss: set $\theta_{i+1}$ to the supplied selector's choice from $\arg\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{r=1}^i\hat L_r(\theta)$.

The finite-sample output is the sequence $\hat\pi_1,\ldots,\hat\pi_N$ and the aggregated labeled dataset. The population-loss idealization replaces each empirical $\hat L_i$ by $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$; it is used only for the infinite-sample theorem. The procedure requires an interactive expert capable of labeling learner-visited states.

lem-dagger-strongly-convex-follow-the-le.interface:
## Statement

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and convex, and define $\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{r=1}^d(x_r-y_r)^2)^{1/2}$. Let $G\ge0$ and $\mu>0$. For each $i=1,\ldots,N$, let $L_i:K\to[0,1]$ be $G$-Lipschitz, meaning $|L_i(x)-L_i(y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2$, and $\mu$-strongly convex, meaning

$$L_i((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le(1-\lambda)L_i(x)+\lambda L_i(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2$$

for all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, assume $F_n:=\sum_{i=1}^nL_i$ attains a minimum on $K$. Let $\theta_1\in K$ and, for $n=1,\ldots,N$, let $\theta_{n+1}$ be the unique minimizer of $F_n$. Define $H_0=0$ and $H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n1/j$ for $n\ge1$. Then

$$\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{i=1}^NL_i(\theta)\le1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}.$$

The minimizers are unique because $F_n$ is $n\mu$-strongly convex. The first policy $\theta_1$ may be any supplied point of $K.

lem-dagger-mixture-occupancy.interface:
## Statement

Let a finite-horizon MDP have positive integer horizon $T$, and let $\pi^*$ and $\hat\pi$ be stationary Markov policies. For a stationary policy $\pi$, define its state transition matrix by $P_\pi(s,s')=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a)$; for a state vector $\mu$, define $(\mu P_\pi)(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)P_\pi(s,s')$. Fix $\beta\in[0,1]$ and let $\pi_\beta(a\mid s)=\beta\pi^*(a\mid s)+(1-\beta)\hat\pi(a\mid s)$, which is the per-decision expert/learner mixture. For every function $g:S\to[0,1]$, its finite-horizon average occupancies satisfy

$$\left|\sum_{s\in S}d_{\pi_\beta}(s)g(s)-\sum_{s\in S}d_{\hat\pi}(s)g(s)\right|\le1-(1-\beta)^T\le\min\{1,T\beta\}.$$

Here $d_\pi=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mu_t^\pi$ is the normalized average of the state marginals from the common initial distribution.

lem-dagger-task-cost-from-expert-surroga.interface:
## Statement

Let a finite-horizon MDP, horizon $T\ge1$, initial distribution, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner policy $\pi_\theta$, task cost $J$, expert cost-to-go $Q_t^*$, expert value $V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s))$, occupancy $d_{\pi_\theta}$, and surrogate $\ell(s,\theta)$ be as defined previously. Suppose $u\ge0$ and

$$Q_t^*(s,a)-V_t^*(s)\le u$$

for every time $0\le t<T$, state $s\in S$, and admissible action $a\in A(s)$, and suppose $\ell(s,\theta)\ge\sum_{a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ for every state. Then

$$J(\pi_\theta)-J(\pi^*)\le uT\sum_{s\in S}d_{\pi_\theta}(s)\ell(s,\theta).$$

The one-step cost-to-go bound is required at all states and times, including states not reached by the expert.

def-martingale-submartingale-and-superma.interface:
## Definition

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. An integrable adapted real process $X$ [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]] is a **martingale**, **submartingale**, or **supermartingale** when, respectively, for every $n\ge0$,
$$E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
These are three separate conditions, with the convention that a submartingale has conditional future mean at least its present value. The conditional expectations are the almost-sure classes of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; that supplier inherits AC from its Radon–Nikodym existence proof. The definition itself selects no representative and assumes no completed filtration.

The condition is imposed at each adjacent pair of times. An all-pairs formulation requires a proof. No boundedness or independence is part of this definition, and no trivial or deterministic initial value is imposed.

thm-martingales-and-martingale-differenc.interface:
## Statement

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale, then $D_n=M_n-M_{n-1}$, $n\ge1$, is a martingale difference sequence. Conversely, given a martingale difference sequence $D$ and any integrable $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real $M_0$, the process $M_n=M_0+\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$ is a martingale. For fixed $M_0$ these constructions are inverse.

def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse.interface:
## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

def-finite-straight-line-computational-p.interface:
## Definition

Fix an input dimension $n\ge0$, finitely many operation nodes $1,\ldots,T$, and a designated output node $o$, either an input coordinate or an operation, whose value space is $\mathbb R$. Give input coordinate $i$ a label $\mathrm{in}_i$ distinct from all operation indices, and set $z_{\mathrm{in}_i}=x_i$ and $E_{\mathrm{in}_i}=\mathbb R$ with its standard Euclidean inner product. Operation node $j$ has an ordered list of parent slots $p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,r_j}$; each slot is either an input label $\mathrm{in}_i$ or an operation index $\ell<j$. Repeated parent slots are allowed and count separately. The graph is a finite straight-line program because every operation reads only earlier values and there are no data-dependent loops.

For each operation $j$, choose a dimension $d_j\ge0$, set $E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$ with its standard Euclidean inner product, take an open set $U_j\subseteq E_{p_{j,1}}\times\cdots\times E_{p_{j,r_j}}$ with the product inner product, and choose a primitive map $\phi_j:U_j\to E_j$. A smooth primitive is $C^1$: it is totally differentiable and its derivative matrix is continuous. For Hessian-vector products require the primitive to be $C^2$, meaning $C^1$ with a continuously differentiable derivative map. Derivatives are represented in these coordinates, and every transpose is the Euclidean transpose for the stated inner products; the gradient of a scalar output is the Euclidean gradient. The real-arithmetic primal recursion is $z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$ whenever the parent tuple lies in $U_j$. Its admissible input domain is the set of $x\in\mathbb R^n$ for which every operation in this recursion is defined. The graph's scalar output function $f$ is the value at $o$: it is $x_i$ when $o$ is input coordinate $i$, and $z_j$ when $o$ is operation node $j$.

The **primal tape** is the finite ordered record of input and node values, parent-slot indices, primitive identities, and (when applicable) selected branch labels. A deterministic replay starts from the identical checkpoint state and applies the identical primitive maps in the identical order, so it reproduces the same real-arithmetic values and local derivative inputs. Opaque solver calls are not primitive operations unless their complete deterministic map and derivative rule are explicitly supplied.

A piecewise-$C^1$ primitive is specified by finitely many open branch regions and a $C^1$ formula on each region; its primal boundary value, if any, is specified separately. If the current parent tuple lies strictly inside exactly one declared branch, the program uses that branch and its derivative. At a branch boundary or ambiguous branch selection, forward or reverse AD returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE; it does not silently choose a subgradient or generalized derivative. If no primal value is specified at a boundary, that input is outside the program's domain. All correctness theorems below apply on a fixed strict branch. The same convention applies to piecewise-$C^2$ primitives for Hessian-vector products.

alg-forward-over-reverse-hessian-vector-.interface:
## Definition

Input a $C^2$ graph, a point $x$, and direction $v$. Run [[alg-forward-mode-automatic-differentiation]] and retain its primal tape and all input and operation tangents. If that call returns DOMAIN_ERROR or NONDIFFERENTIABLE, return the same status and stop without a Hessian-vector product. Otherwise initialize every operation and input cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulator to zero. Seed the output by setting its cotangent/tangent-cotangent pair to $(1,0)$: if $o$ is an operation, set $(\bar z_o,\dot{\bar z}_o)=(1,0)$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)=(1,0)$. In reverse topological order, for each node $j$ and parent slot $k$, let $A_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$, compute
$$c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\bar z_j,\qquad \dot c_{j,k}=A_{j,k}^{T}\dot{\bar z}_j+\bigl(DA_{j,k}(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})[\dot z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,\dot z_{p_{j,r_j}}]\bigr)^{T}\bar z_j,$$
and add $c_{j,k}$ and $\dot c_{j,k}$ to the parent's cotangent and tangent-cotangent accumulators. Use $(\bar x_i,\dot{\bar x}_i)$ for input coordinate $i$ and $(\bar z_\ell,\dot{\bar z}_\ell)$ for operation node $\ell$. If the same parent occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution.
Return $(\dot{\bar x}_1,\ldots,\dot{\bar x}_n)$. Repeated parent slots receive separate additions. The admissible case requires every primitive evaluation to be in its declared domain and, for a piecewise primitive, on a unique strict active branch; a branch boundary or ambiguous selection returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE through the initial call. The transpose is the real Euclidean transpose, not a complex adjoint.

alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiati.interface:
## Definition

Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]] and an admissible point $x$. Require every primitive to be $C^1$ on its declared open domain or supplied as a piecewise-$C^1$ primitive with the branch rules of the graph definition. Evaluate and store all primal values in topological order. Initialize every operation cotangent and every input cotangent to zero. Seed the scalar output by setting its cotangent to $1$: if $o$ is an operation, set $\bar z_o=1$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $\bar x_i=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, compute the contribution
$$c_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})^T\bar z_j$$
and add it to the cotangent accumulator of that parent: use $\bar x_i$ if the parent is input coordinate $i$, and $\bar z_\ell$ if it is operation node $\ell$. If the same parent node occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution. Return the scalar output $f(x)$ and the input cotangents $(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n)$ as the Euclidean gradient. A point outside the admissible domain returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. The procedure differentiates the real-arithmetic graph; it makes no floating-point error claim.

cor-hessian-is-symmetric.interface:
## Statement

For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

def-smooth-bilevel-learning-problem.interface:
## Definition

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

thm-forward-over-reverse-computes-hessia.interface:
## Statement

Let $f$ be the scalar output of a finite $C^2$ graph on a fixed strict branch. At every admissible $x$ and direction $v$, the forward-over-reverse algorithm returns $D(\operatorname{grad} f)(x)v$, the Hessian-vector product $H_f(x)v$. No Hessian symmetry assumption is needed for this identity.

thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient.interface:
## Statement

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem.interface:
## Statement

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

alg-adjoint-hypergradient-with-residual.interface:
## Definition

Input positive dimensions $p,d$, open sets $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $C^2$ and $C^1$ scalar functions $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, a point $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, and finite real-arithmetic computational graphs whose outputs equal $f$ and $g$ on open neighborhoods of the evaluated inputs. The graph primitives for $f$ are $C^2$ and those for $g$ are $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and all graph evaluations must remain on one unique strict branch. Define $F=\nabla_w f$, $H=D_wF$, $B=D_\theta F$, $c=\partial_\theta g$ with $w$ held fixed, and $d=\nabla_w g$; all gradients are column vectors. Also input a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a positive integer solve budget $N$, a number $\mu>0$, and a valid certificate that the evaluated inner Hessian is symmetric and satisfies $x^THx\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Finally input a deterministic solver $S$ with the following contract: on a real symmetric positive-definite linear operator and a right-hand side, $S$ terminates within $N$ iterations and returns either a failure status or a vector $\widetilde v$ and a report saying whether its own stopping test passed. The algorithm does not trust that report as an accuracy certificate; it recomputes the residual. All derivative and solver operations in this definition use exact real arithmetic.

If any graph evaluation is outside its declared domain, return DOMAIN_ERROR. If any piecewise primitive is at a branch boundary or has no unique strict active branch, return NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. Otherwise, use reverse mode on $f$ and take the state block of its returned gradient as the inner residual $r_{\rm in}:=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Use reverse mode on $g$ and take its parameter and state blocks as $c:=\partial_\theta g(w,\theta)$ and $d:=\nabla_w g(w,\theta)$. In these expressions $c$ is the derivative with $w$ held fixed, and $d$ and $c$ are column vectors.

For any $u\in\mathbb R^d$, apply forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector differentiation to $f$ at $(\theta,w)$ in direction $(0,u)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^d$. Let $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_w$ denote projection onto the parameter and state coordinates of the returned vector. Define $M_Hu:=\pi_w\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$ and $M_Bu:=\pi_\theta\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$. Hessian symmetry makes $M_Hu=Hu=H^Tu$ and $M_Bu=B^Tu$.

Call $S$ on $M_H$ and right-hand side $d$ with tolerance $\tau$ and budget $N$. If $S$ returns failure, return $(r_{\rm in},\text{SOLVER\_FAILURE})$ with no hypergradient. If it returns a vector $\widetilde v$, compute the actual linear residual $\rho:=d-M_H\widetilde v$ and the reported hypergradient estimate $\widehat h:=c-M_B\widetilde v$. Return $(\widehat h,r_{\rm in},\rho,\text{CONVERGED})$ exactly when the solver reports its stopping test passed and $\|\rho\|_2\le\tau$; otherwise return the same numerical values with status TOLERANCE_OR_BUDGET_NOT_MET. The procedure makes no floating-point accuracy claim.

lem-implicit-sensitivity-error-controlle.interface:
## Statement

Let $R(z,\theta)$ be $C^2$ near an exact solution $R(z_*,\theta_0)=0$, with $A(z)=R_z(z,\theta_0)$ invertible and $B(z)=R_\theta(z,\theta_0)$. The implicit sensitivity at a state $z$ is $S(z)=-A(z)^{-1}B(z)$. Suppose the local inverse $\Psi$ of $z\mapsto R(z,\theta_0)$, supplied near $z_*$ by the implicit function theorem, is defined on a convex residual neighborhood containing $0$ and $r=R(\tilde z,\theta_0)$, with $\|D\Psi(y)\|\le\kappa$ along their segment. Suppose also that the segment from $z_*$ to $\tilde z=\Psi(r)$ lies in a convex neighborhood where $\|A(z)^{-1}\|\le M$, $\|B(z)\|\le B_0$, and $A,B$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_A,L_B$. Then
$$\|S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)\|\le\kappa\bigl(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B\bigr)\|r\|.$$
This bounds the implicit sensitivity formula evaluated at an approximate state. It is not by itself a bound for the derivative of a stopped iteration.

thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-deri.interface:
## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

thm-smooth-bilevel-hypergradient-formula.interface:
## Statement

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, and $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$. Define $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$, $H(\theta,w)=D_wF(\theta,w)$, and $B(\theta,w)=D_\theta F(\theta,w)$. Suppose $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$ and $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $\theta_0$ and $w_0$ and a unique $C^1$ local stationary branch $w^*:P\to Q$ through $(\theta_0,w_0)$, meaning $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for every $\theta\in P$. After shrinking $P$ if necessary, $H(\theta,w^*(\theta))$ is invertible and

$$Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta)).$$

Write $H^{-T}:=(H^{-1})^T$. For $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, where $\partial_\theta g$ holds $w$ fixed and gradients are column vectors, the hypergradient is

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\partial_\theta g(w^*(\theta),\theta)-B(\theta,w^*(\theta))^T H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-T}\nabla_w g(w^*(\theta),\theta).$$

The local branch need not be a global inner optimizer. In the separate global regime where, for every $\theta\in P$, $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for some $\mu>0$, satisfies $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, each stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

thm-finite-iteration-sensitivity-bound-a.interface:
## Statement

Let $p,m\ge0$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $\theta_0\in\Theta$, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\Theta$ of $D\times\{\theta_0\}$. Suppose $D\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is an open convex neighborhood of $z_*$ and $z_*=G(z_*,\theta_0)$. Assume $G(D,\theta_0)\subseteq D$, $\|G_z(z,\theta_0)\|\le q<1$ on $D$, and $G_z,G_\theta$ are Lipschitz in $z$ with constants $L_z,L_\theta$. Let $z_0:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, with the iterates at $\theta_0$ lying in $D$. Write $s_*=D\phi(\theta_0)$ for the local exact fixed-point branch (supplied by the implicit function theorem when $p,m\ge1$), $e_k=D_\theta z_k(\theta_0)$, $\delta_0=\|z_0(\theta_0)-z_*\|$, $d_0=\|e_0-s_*\|$, and $C=L_z\|s_*\|+L_\theta$. For every integer $K\ge1$,
$$\|z_K(\theta_0)-z_*\|\le q^K\delta_0,\qquad \|e_K-s_*\|\le q^K d_0+C K q^{K-1}\delta_0,$$
with $q^0=1$ when $q=0,K=1$. If $R(z,\theta)=z-G(z,\theta)$ and $r_K=R(z_K(\theta_0),\theta_0)$, then $(1-q)\|z_K-z_*\|\le\|r_K\|$. The derivative error is not bounded by the residual alone: for $G(z,\theta)=qz+(1-q)\theta$, $\theta_0=0$, and $z_0(\theta)=0$, every finite $K$ has residual zero at $\theta_0$ but $e_K=1-q^K\ne1=s_*$ when $0<q<1$.

rem-truncated-training-and-exact-hypergr.interface:
## Boundary

Let $p,m\ge0$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $\theta_0\in\Theta$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an open convex neighborhood of $z_*$, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood $U$ of $D\times\{\theta_0\}$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and vector and operator norms are Euclidean and induced Euclidean norms. Write $G_z:=D_zG$ and $G_\theta:=D_\theta G$ for the state and parameter derivatives. Suppose $z_*=G(z_*,\theta_0)$, $G(D,\theta_0)\subseteq D$, $0\le q<1$, $\|G_z(z,\theta_0)\|\le q$ on $D$, and $G_z,G_\theta$ are Lipschitz in $z$ with constants $L_z,L_\theta$. Let $z_0:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, with all finite iterates at $\theta_0$ lying in $D$, and define $z_{k+1}(\theta)=G(z_k(\theta),\theta)$. Let $\phi$ be the exact local fixed-point branch, $s_*:=D\phi(\theta_0)$, $e_K:=Dz_K(\theta_0)$, $\delta_0:=\|z_0(\theta_0)-z_*\|_2$, $d_0:=\|Dz_0(\theta_0)-s_*\|$, and $C:=L_z\|s_*\|+L_\theta$. For every integer $K\ge1$,

$$\|e_K-s_*\|\le q^K d_0+C K q^{K-1}\delta_0,$$

where $q^0=1$ when $q=0$ and $K=1$. For the fixed-point residual $r_K:=z_K(\theta_0)-G(z_K(\theta_0),\theta_0)$, the primal-state estimate is $(1-q)\|z_K(\theta_0)-z_*\|_2\le\|r_K\|_2$. This primal residual estimate alone does not imply that the derivative of the finite $K$-step graph equals the exact fixed-point sensitivity.

For a separate finite shared-parameter recurrence, let $p_0,q_0\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\mathbb R^{p_0}$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^{q_0}$ be open, let $T\ge0$, let $h_0:\Theta_0\to H$ and $\Phi_t:\Theta_0\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$ and $\ell:\Theta_0\times H\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta_0$, and suppose every piecewise primitive is evaluated in one unique strict open $C^1$ branch. Set $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $J_T(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$; derivative matrices use Euclidean coordinates and transposes are Euclidean. Backpropagation differentiates this finite scalar graph: with $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$, and $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$, its derivative is

$$\nabla_\theta J_T(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^T A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0.$$

This is the derivative of the finite training computation. The exact implicit hypergradient is the derivative of a local stationary or fixed-point branch. In particular, a small training residual is not by itself an error bound for the derivative of a stopped iteration; contraction and sensitivity hypotheses such as those stated above are needed.

## Boundary references

[[thm-shared-parameter-backpropagation-gradient-formula|Gradient of a finite shared-parameter recurrence]]

[[alg-adjoint-hypergradient-with-residual|Adjoint solve and measured residual]]
